Chapter 1 is pure theory, and almost every question is an 8-mark question split 4+4, 3+5 or 2+6: two lists glued together. Learn the lists below as lists.
  1. Six lists carry the chapter, each asked in 9 to 16 papers: importance of organization, principles of organization, formal vs informal organization, functions of management, levels + skills of management, and the three classical theories (Taylor, Fayol, Mayo).
  2. Forms of ownership and structures are compare-and-choose questions: “JSC vs partnership”, “line & staff vs line”, “which structure for an engineering project”. The comparison tables in \(\S\)1.4 and \(\S\)1.5 answer them directly.
  3. Purchasing and marketing: two questions set every year in some form (functions of purchasing; importance of marketing).

column1: Define organization. Why is it necessary? Explain its importance and role in society
column2: 123458
column4:
Definition
  • Mooney and Reiley: “Organization is the form of every human association for the attainment of a common purpose.”
  • Working definition: a collection of people working together in a coordinated and structured way to achieve one or more goals.
  • As a process: identifying + grouping work \(\rightarrow\) defining + delegating responsibility and authority \(\rightarrow\) establishing relationships so people work effectively together.
  • Three views of the same thing (AJ Sir): goal-oriented system (people work for specific goals), social system (people work in groups), technological system (people apply knowledge and techniques).
Necessity (why we need organization)
  • Complexity of industry: large plants, complex methods need structure.
  • Growing competition: required quantity + quality, at required time, at minimum cost.
  • Optimum use of resources: men, machines, materials, money.
  • Fixes authority and responsibility \(\rightarrow\) no confusion, no conflict.
  • Coordination of efforts of many people toward one goal.
  • Reduces labour problems; facilitates administration.
  • Stimulates creativity and specialization.
  • People achieve together what no individual can alone; diverse skills, more resources.
  • Andrew Carnegie: take away the money and the works but leave the organization, and he would rebuild within a few years.
Importance / role in society
  • Produces goods and services society needs (food, power, transport).
  • Employment and income \(\rightarrow\) livelihood for millions.
  • Development: hospitals, schools, universities, banks, telecom, roads.
  • Raises living standard: better products at lower cost.
  • Innovation and technology: research, new products.
  • Revenue to government (taxes) \(\rightarrow\) public services.
  • Social welfare: CSR, cooperatives, NGOs serve the weak.
  • Civilization itself is organized effort: without organization there is only self-sufficiency, no division of labour, no trade.
  • Can we sustain without organization? No: every need beyond bare survival (education, health, security) is delivered by some organization.

column1: Role of organization in an employee's professional growth
column4:
• Training and development: on-the-job training, workshops, higher study.
  • Career path: promotion through levels, job rotation, wider responsibility.
  • Performance appraisal / merit rating \(\rightarrow\) feedback, recognition.
  • Mentoring: seniors and supervisors transfer knowledge (knowledge-oriented model).
  • Exposure: teamwork, projects, clients, new technology build skills.
  • Security + remuneration: stable income lets an employee invest in learning.

column1: Organization as a system: open system, social system, system approach applied to organization
column4:
• System = set of interdependent parts working together toward a goal.
  • Organization as a system:
    • Inputs: 5 M's, men, materials, machines, money, methods (+ information).
    • Transformation process: sub-systems (production, finance, marketing, personnel) convert inputs.
    • Outputs: products, services, profit, employee satisfaction.
    • Feedback: customer response, results vs plan \(\rightarrow\) corrections.
    • Environment: external (social, political, economic, cultural, technology) and internal (board, employees, culture).
  • Open system: continuously exchanges inputs and outputs with its environment and must adapt to changes in technology, market, customer needs, rules. A closed system ignores the environment and decays.
  • Social system: people interact in groups; their attitudes, perceptions, norms shape how it works (Mayo, Barnard).
  • System approach applied: every change (new technology, process) ripples to people, jobs, skills \(\rightarrow\) plan for change, assess change forces, implement (Kaila). Also called a change-management plan.
Organization as an open system: inputs, transforming sub-systems, outputs, feedback from both ends. ioenotes Ch. 1, p1.
Organizations, people and management
  • Organizations exist to accomplish work people cannot do alone.
  • While their goals stay appropriate, society lets them exist.
  • People shape organizations: their personality, attitudes and behaviour decide how it operates.
  • Organizations need management to achieve their goals.

column1: Principles of organization
column4:
1. Unity of objectives: clear goals for firm, each department, each post.
  2. Division of labour / specialization: work split into jobs matched to skill.
  3. Departmentalization: related activities grouped into units.
  4. Scalar chain / chain of command: clear line of authority top to bottom.
  5. Unity of command: one subordinate, one boss.
  6. Authority = responsibility: authority given must match duty assigned.
  7. Span of control: limited no. of subordinates per supervisor (5–6 at top, up to 20 at shop floor).
  8. Delegation: authority pushed down to where decisions are made.
  1. Centralization vs decentralization balanced to firm size.
  2. Coordination: departments' work synchronized.
  3. Simplicity: minimum levels \(\rightarrow\) easy communication.
  4. Flexibility: structure adapts to growth and change.
  5. Communication: free two-way flow, with feedback.
  6. Continuity: structure survives change of people.
  7. Efficiency: goals at minimum cost and effort.
Examples (for 82 Bh)
  • Unity of command: a hospital ward nurse reports to one ward in-charge only.
  • Span of control: a factory foreman supervises 15 workers, a CEO only 5 managers.
  • Unity of objectives: a bank splits its national target into branch targets.
  • Scalar chain: a site engineer's leave request goes through the project manager, not straight to the MD.
Two cautions worth a line
  • Over-specialization: jobs split too finely become boring \(\rightarrow\) performance falls. Balance specialization with job rotation or enlargement.
  • Span keeps widening: with downsizing and IT, firms remove layers \(\rightarrow\) each manager supervises more people.
  • Flexibility means small alterations and expansions as circumstances change, not a new structure every year.
How to write the 8-mark version
  • Name 8 principles, one line each.
  • Give each a one-line example.
  • Close with one line on why they matter: clear roles, no duplication, faster decisions.

column1: Formal and informal organization: definitions, differences, need for informal organization
column4:
• Formal organization: structure deliberately created by management for enterprise objectives; official network of authority, responsibility and communication. Chester Barnard: “a system of consciously coordinated activities of two or more persons towards a common objective”; exists when people (a) can communicate, (b) are willing to act, (c) share a purpose.
  • Informal organization: network of personal and social relations that emerges spontaneously from friendship, language, culture, common interests. Barnard: “joint personal activity without conscious common purpose, though contributing to joint results”. Has its own informal leader, norms and grapevine.
BasisFormalInformal
OriginDeliberately created by managementSpontaneous, social and psychological forces
PurposeOrganization's legitimate goalsMembers' social satisfaction
SizeCan be very largeSmall groups
StabilityStable, long-livedUnstable
AuthorityHierarchy, flows top downAll equal; power flows from the group
BehaviourRules and regulationsGroup norms, beliefs, values
CommunicationOfficial chain of commandGrapevine, informal channels
LeadershipVested in the managerChosen by the group, may out-power the manager
AbolitionManagement can abolish itManagement cannot abolish it
ChartShown on organization chartNever shown
Need for informal organization (“do we need it indeed?”)
  • Yes: it fills gaps the formal structure leaves.
  • Social satisfaction, sense of belonging \(\rightarrow\) morale.
  • Fast communication (grapevine) across departments.
  • Cooperation and teamwork beyond job descriptions.
  • Safety valve for frustration; eases work pressure.
  • Feedback to management on real employee mood.
  • Risks: rumours, resistance to change, group conflict. Management should understand and use it, not suppress it (Hawthorne, \(\S\)1.3).
Informal organization within the same family? (79 Ba)
  • Yes. A family is itself an informal organization (no written hierarchy), yet sub-groups form inside it: siblings, cousins of the same age, members sharing a hobby or a family business.
  • In a family business (single owner or partnership) the formal roles (owner, manager, accountant) sit alongside informal family loyalties, which often decide more than the formal roles do.

column1: Historical development of organization
column4:
• Concept of organization grew with economic activity: each stage needed a larger, more structured way of working together.
1. Pre-industrial era
  • Self-sufficiency (village economy).
  • Commercial stage with marketable surplus: barter \(\rightarrow\) money system.
  • Means of transport (ships, railways) \(\rightarrow\) wider trade.
2. Modern industrial era
  • Industrial revolution (James Watt's steam engine, machine tools) \(\rightarrow\) factories.
  • Corporate form: joint stock company with limited liability.
  • Managerial revolution: scientific management (Taylor, Fayol).
  • Mechanization, automation; economic liberalization.
  • Globalization: multinationals; GATT (1947), ISO (1947), WTO (1995), SAFTA.

column1: Organizational behaviour: a multidisciplinary field; how management affects it
column4:
• OB = study of how individuals and groups behave in organizations, to improve performance and satisfaction.
  • Multidisciplinary, it borrows from:
    • Psychology: individual learning, motivation, perception, personality.
    • Sociology: groups, roles, status, culture.
    • Social psychology: attitude change, group decisions, communication.
    • Anthropology: values, cultures across societies.
    • Political science: power, conflict, politics in organizations.
How management affects OB
  • Structure: tall, rigid hierarchy \(\rightarrow\) caution and passing the buck; flat structure \(\rightarrow\) initiative.
  • Leadership style: autocratic control breeds compliance; participation breeds commitment.
  • Reward system: what is rewarded gets repeated.
  • Job design: enriched jobs raise interest; monotonous jobs raise absenteeism.
  • Communication and culture: open channels build trust; rumours fill silence.

column1: Define management. Explain the functions of management
column4:
• Simple: getting things done through other people.
  • Full: “a social process involving coordination of human and material resources through planning, organizing, staffing, leading and controlling, to accomplish stated objectives” effectively (right goals) and efficiently (least resources).
  • Resources it coordinates: people, machinery, raw materials, computers and IT, patents, finance, loyal customers.
  • The brain of an organization; as old as civilization (Sun Tzu, Chanakya's Arthashastra).
  • Efficiency = doing things right (least input per output). Effectiveness = doing the right things (the goal customers want). High performers are both (figure).
Efficiency (use of resources) across, effectiveness (choice of goal) down.
  • Management is an ongoing activity made of eight functions (Adhikari), detailed below.
  • They form a process, not a sequence done once: evaluation feeds revised plans and changed procedures (right).
  • Fayol's five (AJ Sir): planning, organizing, directing (commanding), coordinating, controlling. Write these five if the question says “basic” functions.
The management process as a loop.
Functions (POSDCoRB, extended)
  1. Planning: “thinking before doing”.
    • Deciding in advance what, how, when and by whom (Koontz & O'Donnell).
    • Sets objectives and the path to them; basis of every other function.
    • Eg a hydropower firm fixes its commissioning date and budget.
  2. Organizing: the backbone of management.
    • Identify and group activities into departments and jobs.
    • Assign them to people; set authority-responsibility relations.
  3. Staffing: filling the posts of the structure.
    • Recruit, select, place, train, appraise, pay (Ch. 2).
    • Right person in the right job at the right time.
  4. Directing: putting the plan into action.
    • Orders, guidance, supervision of subordinates.
    • Needs leadership and communication, not just commands.
  1. Motivating: stimulating willingness to work.
    • Uses internal (interest, pride) and external (pay, praise) motivators.
    • Satisfied needs \(\rightarrow\) effort and loyalty (Ch. 3).
  2. Coordinating: “orderly arrangement of group effort to provide unity of action” (Mooney & Reiley).
    • Synchronizes departments so no one works against another.
    • Internal, external, vertical, horizontal.
  3. Controlling: checking results against plans.
    • Set standards, measure performance, correct deviations.
    • Physical, financial and budgetary control.
  4. Communicating: the link through which all others work.
    • Sender, message, receiver, feedback.
    • Orders flow down, reports and suggestions flow up.

column1: Planning: meaning, objectives, steps, advantages, limitations, components
column4:
• Meaning: most basic function; thinking before doing; preparation for action.
  • Includes forecasting and framing objectives, policies, programs, schedules, procedures, budgets.
  • Koontz and O'Donnell: “deciding in advance what to do, how to do it, when to do it and who is to do it. Planning bridges the gap from where we are to where we want to go.”
Objectives of planning
  1. Effective forecasting: anticipate demand, costs, risks.
  2. Certainty in activities: everyone knows what comes next.
  3. Performance standards: targets that control can measure against.
  4. Specific direction: all departments pull toward one goal.
  5. Tune the organization to its environment: market, policy, technology.
  6. Economy in management: no idle resources, no duplicated effort.
Advantages
  • Maximum use of resources; reduces uncertainty.
  • Basis for managerial action and for control.
  • Encourages innovation and creativity.
Limitations
  • Forecasts can be wrong.
  • Costly and time consuming.
  • External factors (policy, market, disaster) upset plans.
  • Resistance to change; rigidity and inflexibility.
Components of planning from the broadest (goals) to the most numerical (budgets).

column1: Organizing and staffing: meaning and steps
column4:
• Organizing: identify and group activities, divide them among people, create authority-responsibility relationships among them.
  • The backbone of management: links people, work and resources.
  • Avoids duplication and gaps: every task has an owner.
  • Staffing: fill the posts of the structure with competent, qualified people (detail in Ch. 2).
  • Continuous: people retire, leave or are promoted, so posts keep reopening.

column1: Directing and motivating
column4:
Directing
  • Motivating, guiding and supervising subordinates toward company objectives.
  • Only giving orders is not directing: plans succeed only when diverse human efforts are coordinated, guided and directed.
  • It actuates members to work effectively and efficiently.
  • Steps:
    1. issue orders and instructions;
    2. guide and train subordinates;
    3. supervise their work.
  • Elements: supervision, communication, leadership, motivation.
Motivating: fundamentals
  • Inspiring people to intensify their desire and willingness to perform and co-operate; “push the right button to get the desired action”.
  • First fundamental: people want to exist and survive: food, clothing, shelter, education, medical care.
  • Second: the desire to achieve a goal: psychological, social, security, ego (self-respect) needs. People work sincerely when sure these will be met.
Essentials of a sound motivation system
  1. Good wages: enough for a decent living.
  2. Financial incentives: bonus, profit share linked to output.
  3. Achievement and growth: training, promotion paths.
  4. Human relations: respect, recognition, fair treatment.
  5. Good working conditions: safety, light, rest.
  6. Job satisfaction: interesting, meaningful work.
  7. Job security: no fear of arbitrary dismissal.

column1: Controlling and co-ordinating
column4:
Controlling
  • Setting standards, measuring actual performance, taking corrective action.
  • Koontz and O'Donnell: “measurement of accomplishment against the standard and correction of deviations to ensure attainment of objectives according to plans.”
  • Types, by objective:
    • physical: quantity and quality of products;
    • financial: unit cost, material cost, labour expense;
    • budgetary: future physical and financial standards set, results compared.
Co-ordinating
  • Ongoing process by which a manager develops an integrated, orderly, synchronized pattern of group effort, for unity of effort toward a common purpose.
  • Mooney and Reiley: “the orderly arrangement of group effort, to provide unity of action in the pursuit of common purpose.”
  • Achieved through clear objectives, sound structure, communication, committees, leadership.
Types of co-ordination

• Process by which instructions, ideas, thoughts or information are transmitted, received and understood by people in the organization.
  • Components: sender, message, receiver, feedback.
  • Sender prepares the message properly; receiver must understand it clearly.

column1: Two principal functions and why they matter most (79 Ba)
column4:
• Choose planning and controlling: the two ends of the same loop.
  • Planning:
    • Sets the target, the method and the timetable.
    • Every other function starts from it: organizing groups the work the plan needs, staffing fills it, directing executes it.
    • Reduces uncertainty and waste.
  • Controlling:
    • Checks the result against the plan.
    • Catches deviations early, while they are cheap to fix.
    • Feeds lessons into the next plan.
  • Why these two: no plan \(\rightarrow\) nothing to control; no control \(\rightarrow\) plans are only wishes.

column1: Levels of management: why different levels are needed, and functions at each level
column4:
• Top level (board of directors, CEO, MD, chairman):
    • Sets goals, objectives, policies, budget.
    • Main function: decision making, planning; cross-department responsibility.
    • Answerable for success or failure of the whole firm.
  • Middle level (department heads, section officers):
    • Implements top's policies; organizes resources.
    • Link between top and lower; plans for own department.
    • Selects, trains, motivates lower managers.
  • Lower / operative level (foreman, supervisor, inspector):
    • Day-to-day supervision of workers; directing and on-the-spot control.
    • Passes workers' problems upward.
Authority rises and responsibility widens toward the top. AJ Sir, Ch. 1 deck, slide 15.
Why levels are needed
  • Span of control: one person cannot direct hundreds.
  • Division of work: strategic vs tactical vs operational decisions.
  • Clear authority and responsibility; accountability at each step.
  • Communication: orders down, reports up.
  • Specialization and career growth: a ladder for managers.
Share of time on each function by level: top managers plan and organize most; first-line managers lead (direct) most.

column1: Managerial skills and the degree needed at each level; qualities of a good manager
column4:
Katz's three skills
  • Technical skill: job-specific methods, processes, tools, equipment of a specialized field. Most needed at lower level.
  • Human (interpersonal) skill: understand, communicate with, motivate and lead people and groups. Needed equally at all levels.
  • Conceptual skill: see the organization as a whole, analyse and diagnose situations, cause vs effect, long-range decisions. Most needed at top.
Modern manager also needs
  • Decision-making, communication, IT / digital skills.
  • Time management, diagnostic skill, design skill (solving problems, not just spotting them).
Degree of each skill by level: conceptual shrinks and technical grows going down; human skill stays wide throughout.
Qualities of a good manager
  • Leadership and vision: sees where the unit must go, carries people along.
  • Decisiveness: decides on time with incomplete information.
  • Communication: clear orders, and listens to subordinates.
  • Integrity and fairness: treats all alike; earns trust.
  • Technical knowledge of the field, and the ability to keep learning.
  • Emotional stability: calm under pressure; patient.
  • Initiative: acts on problems before being told.

column1: Roles of a manager (Mintzberg)
column4:
• Interpersonal roles:
    • Figurehead: ceremonial head; signs documents, receives visitors.
    • Leader: hires, trains, motivates subordinates.
    • Liaison: builds a network outside the unit.
  • Informational roles:
    • Monitor: gathers news about the unit and its environment.
    • Disseminator: passes that information inside.
    • Spokesperson: speaks for the unit to outsiders.
  • Decisional roles:
    • Entrepreneur: spots opportunities, starts change.
    • Disturbance handler: fixes crises, strikes, breakdowns.
    • Resource allocator: decides who gets what money, people, time.
    • Negotiator: bargains with unions, suppliers, clients.
  • AJ Sir's “interpersonal, informational, decisional skills” are these three role groups.

column1: Importance of management
column4:
• Achieves group goals: directs everyone to common objectives.
  • Optimum use of resources: efficient + effective; less waste. The better a society uses scarce resources, the greater its well-being.
  • Reduces costs \(\rightarrow\) competitive prices.
  • Establishes sound organization: right person, right job.
  • Adapts to change: new technology, markets.
  • For individuals: helps people deal with bosses and co-workers; opens a path to a well-paying job and a satisfying career.
  • Development of society: “no underdeveloped countries, only undermanaged ones”; jobs, better living standard.
  • Breaks the poverty cycle: low productivity \(\rightarrow\) low income \(\rightarrow\) low saving \(\rightarrow\) low investment; good management lifts productivity and turns the loop upward (ioenotes p5).

column1: Models of management: name them, explain any two or three with examples
column4:
1. Hierarchical:
    • Authority comes from the superior; responsibility is owed to the superior.
    • Eg army, civil service.
    • Misses: leadership, charisma, informal communication.
  2. Task-oriented:
    • Manager performs five tasks: plan, organize, direct, coordinate, control.
    • The tasks cycle, they are not a line (figure below).
    • Eg a production plant. Misses: can create artificial manager-worker links.
  3. Allocational:
    • Manager obtains, allocates, shares, monitors and returns resources (money, manpower, materials): “keeping the cup topped up”.
    • Eg finance or project resource manager.
    • Misses: no true process view of managing.
  4. Transactional:
    • Management as a stage in the value-added chain; adds value to raw resources.
    • Shows how management adds value, not just control.
    • Eg supply chain firms.
  1. Team effort:
    • Interlocking teams; manager as team leader stressing cooperation and coordination.
    • Team output exceeds the sum of individuals.
    • Leader embodies the group's traits to motivate it.
    • Eg an agile software team, a surgical team.
  2. Knowledge-oriented:
    • Manager builds knowledge by experience, diffuses it by mentoring, teaching, coaching, training.
    • The firm learns to adapt and wins in change.
    • Eg consulting, R&D.
  3. Goal-concentrated:
    • Management as control toward goals, including resource management.
    • Information from the environment triggers adjustments so the plan holds.
    • Eg a sales team with targets.
  • A real firm usually mixes several models.
Hierarchical model (left) and task-oriented model (right).

column1: Management: science or art?
column4:
• Science: systematic body of knowledge; principles (Fayol, Taylor) tested by observation; cause-effect. Eg time study sets a standard output.
  • Inexact science: deals with people, so results are not perfectly repeatable.
  • Art: personal skill, creativity, judgement in applying knowledge; improves with practice. Eg two managers apply the same rule with different success.
  • Both: science gives the principles, art applies them. Complementary.

column1: Organization vs management (vs administration)
column4:
BasisOrganizationManagement
MeaningStructure: people + jobs + relationsProcess: planning, organizing, directing, controlling
NatureA tool / framework (the body)The force that runs it (the brain)
RelationOne function of managementUses organization to reach goals

column1: Which management theory is most practical today / best for organizations in Nepal?
column4:
• Argue for the contingency / system approach: no single best way; mix theories to fit the situation.
  • Why, for Nepal:
    • Mixed sector: family firms, cooperatives, public corporations, MNCs, IT startups \(\rightarrow\) each needs a different style.
    • Labour-intensive manufacturing (garments, cement) \(\rightarrow\) Taylor's time study and incentives still raise output.
    • Public enterprises (NEA, NOC) \(\rightarrow\) Fayol's clear hierarchy, unity of command, discipline cure overlapping authority.
    • Service and IT firms, remittance-driven youth workforce \(\rightarrow\) behavioural approach: motivation, participation, recognition to retain staff.
    • Political instability, frequent policy change \(\rightarrow\) open-system thinking, watching the environment.
  • Conclude: contingency approach, drawing on all the classical tools.

column1: Scientific management (Taylor): principles, experiments, features, applicability today
column4:
• F.W. Taylor (1856–1915), US engineer at Midvale and Bethlehem Steel; “Father of Scientific Management”. Book: Principles of Scientific Management (1911). Term coined by Louis Brandeis (1910); Charles Babbage anticipated it (1832).
  • Definition: “the art of knowing exactly what is to be done and the best way of doing it”; replacing rule of thumb with scientific study of work.
  • Applies scientific knowledge and method to every aspect of management \(\rightarrow\) best use of men, materials, machines, capital.
  • Historical development:
    • Before: rule-of-thumb factories, soldiering (deliberate slow work), no standards.
    • Taylor's shop studies (1880s).
    • Gilbreths' motion study; Gantt chart.
    • Mass production (Ford's assembly line, 1913).
Taylor's own principles
  1. Science, not rule of thumb, for each element of work.
  2. Scientific selection, training and development of workers.
  3. Cooperation, not individualism, between management and labour.
  4. Equal division of responsibility: management plans, workers do.
  5. Harmony, not discord; maximum output, not restricted output.
Adhikari's list of principles (write it if asked “principles” at 8 marks)
  1. Science for each element of work.
  2. Scientific selection, placement and training.
  3. Division of labour.
  4. Standardization of methods and tools.
  5. Time and motion study.
  6. Differential wages.
  7. Labour-management co-operation.
  8. Management by exception.
Techniques (features)
  • Time study: standard time \(\rightarrow\) fair day's work.
  • Motion study: remove wasted motions (Gilbreth).
  • Fatigue study: rest pauses.
  • Standardization of tools, methods, conditions.
  • Differential piece-rate wages: higher rate above standard.
  • Functional foremanship: 8 specialist foremen.
  • Management by exception: only deviations go to top.
Experiments that support it
  • Pig-iron handling (Bethlehem Steel, 1898): 75 labourers loading 42 kg pigs; by method study, rest periods and incentive pay, output rose 12.5 \(\rightarrow\) 47.5 tons/day (AJ Sir's figures: 12.7 \(\rightarrow\) 48.8), wages $1.15 \(\rightarrow\) $1.85.
  • Shovelling: shovel sized to a 21.5 lb load for each material; 400–600 men cut to 140, cost per ton halved.
  • Metal cutting: 26 years, 30,000 tests on speeds, feeds \(\rightarrow\) high-speed steel.
Still applicable today? Yes, largely
  • Assembly lines, fast food, BPO call centres use standard times and methods.
  • Lean manufacturing, Six Sigma, industrial engineering are its heirs.
  • Incentive pay, work study, ERP-based control.
  • But: human needs ignored, monotony, worker resentment \(\rightarrow\) combine with behavioural approach.

column1: Scientific management vs management science
column4:
• Scientific management (Taylor, 1900s): improves worker productivity at shop level by time and motion study, standardization, incentive wages.
  • Management science (quantitative approach, 1940s on): uses mathematical models, operations research, statistics, simulation, linear programming for managerial decisions at every level.
  • Scope: the first studies how a job is done; the second studies what decision to take (how much to stock, which route, which project).
  • Tools: stopwatch, motion charts, piece rates vs computers, mathematical models, queuing, inventory models.
  • Link: management science grew out of Taylor's idea of measuring instead of guessing.

column1: Role of HR manager; how HR manager implements scientific management
column4:
Role / significance of the HR manager (4)
  • Manpower planning: forecasts how many people, of what skill, when.
  • Recruitment and selection: attracts and picks the right candidates.
  • Training and development: builds skills; plans careers.
  • Performance appraisal: measures work, feeds promotion and pay.
  • Wage and salary administration: fair, competitive pay; incentives.
  • Welfare and safety: working conditions, health, canteen, housing.
  • Industrial relations: handles grievances, unions, bargaining.
  • Retention: keeps good staff; records and HR information (see Ch. 2).
How the HR manager implements scientific management (4)
  1. Job analysis: studies each job; writes job description and specification.
  2. Time and motion study: fixes the standard time and the one best method.
  3. Scientific selection: tests and interviews match people to jobs.
  4. Training in the standard method, not rule of thumb.
  5. Standardization: tools, working conditions, rest pauses.
  6. Differential incentive wages: higher rate for output above standard.
  7. Worker-management cooperation: explains the system, shares gains, handles grievances so workers do not resist.
  8. Management by exception: reports only deviations upward.

column1: Administrative management (Fayol): 14 principles, and are they applicable today?
column4:
• Henri Fayol (1841–1925), French mining engineer; “Father of Modern Management”. General and Industrial Management (1916).
  • Studied management from the top down (Taylor: from the shop floor up); set the pattern of management and the pyramidal organization.
  • Technical ability dominates at lower levels; managerial ability at higher levels.
  • Six activities of an industrial undertaking:
    1. Technical: production, manufacture, adaptation.
    2. Commercial: purchasing, selling, exchange.
    3. Financial: optimum use of capital.
    4. Security: protection of property and persons.
    5. Accounting: stock taking, balance sheet, costing, statistics.
    6. Managerial: planning, organizing, commanding, co-ordinating, controlling.
The 14 principles
  1. Division of work: each person does a specialized part \(\rightarrow\) skill, speed, output rise.
  2. Authority and responsibility: go together; whoever has the right to order answers for the result.
  3. Discipline: obedience and respect for agreements; fair penalties; needs good superiors at every level.
  4. Unity of command: orders from one boss only; two bosses \(\rightarrow\) confusion.
  5. Unity of direction: one plan and one head for each group of activities with the same objective.
  6. Subordination of individual interest to the general interest of the firm.
  7. Remuneration: fair to both employee and employer; satisfies both.
  1. Centralization: how far decisions stay at the top; the degree depends on size and situation.
  2. Scalar chain: unbroken line of authority from top to bottom; a “gang plank” lets peers talk directly when speed matters.
  3. Order: a right place for everything and everyone (material and social order).
  4. Equity: kindness plus justice toward all employees \(\rightarrow\) loyalty.
  5. Stability of tenure: low turnover; people need time to learn a job.
  6. Initiative: let subordinates think out and carry out plans.
  7. Esprit de corps: “union is strength”; team spirit and harmony.
Applicable today? Yes
  • Every organization chart uses scalar chain, unity of command, division of work.
  • Fayol's functions (POCCC) are still the standard management process.
  • Matrix structures bend unity of command; startups bend centralization. Principles are flexible guidelines, applied by situation (Fayol said so himself).
Experiments / contributions around it
  • Fayol: 30 years running Commentry-Fourchambault, turned a near-bankrupt mining firm profitable by applying these principles.
  • Frank Gilbreth (father of motion study): process chart; fatigue cut by rest periods, seating layout, better conditions, principles of motion economy; therbligs.
  • Gantt: Gantt chart, a scheduling tool comparing planned vs actual progress at a glance \(\rightarrow\) corrective action on a significant deviation (see the plan chart in \(\S\)4.4).
  • Weber: bureaucracy (rules, hierarchy, impersonality).

column1: Behavioural management approach (Mayo, Hawthorne): and how it compares with scientific and administrative approaches
column4:
• Scientific management concentrated on physical resources, not human ones.
  • Elton Mayo and associates (1920s–30s): organization is a social system, not only a techno-economic one. Productivity depends on human behaviour and social environment, not only money.
  • Good human relations \(\rightarrow\) harmony, higher satisfaction \(\rightarrow\) higher efficiency and productivity.
  • Also: Maslow (need hierarchy), McGregor (X-Y), Herzberg, Follett, Barnard. Human relations movement.
  • Motivators are the job and its conditions: recognition, belonging, challenging work, independence, participation, achievement, job enlargement and enrichment.
Elements of behavioural theory
  1. The individual: recognize individual differences; each person has feelings, emotions, perceptions, attitudes, a changing psychology.
  2. The work group: informal organization matters; integrate it intelligently with the formal one; group psychology drives motivation and productivity.
  3. Participative management: workers share decision making and problem solving, mainly to raise productivity.
Hawthorne experiments (Western Electric, 1924–32)
  1. Illumination (1924–27): output rose whether light went up or down \(\rightarrow\) physical factors were not the cause.
  2. Relay assembly test room: 6 women; rest, hours, pay varied; output rose almost every time \(\rightarrow\) attention, group morale matter.
  3. Interviewing programme: 21,000 workers \(\rightarrow\) feelings, informal groups shape performance.
  4. Bank wiring room: 14 men; group set its own output norm and enforced it \(\rightarrow\) informal group controls output.
Conclusions
  • Attention from managers raises output (Hawthorne effect).
  • Workers are social beings; money is not the only motivator.
  • Informal groups set norms; must be integrated with the formal organization.
  • Satisfaction \(\rightarrow\) productivity; participation and communication matter.
  • Managers need social skills, not only technical ones.
Limitations
  • Over-stresses the social side; satisfied workers are not always productive.
  • Hawthorne method criticized (small samples).
BasisScientific (Taylor)Administrative (Fayol)Behavioural (Mayo)
FocusWorker, shop floorManager, whole firmPeople and groups
View of personEconomic man, money motivatesPart of a structureSocial man, needs motivate
AimMax output per workerSound structure, principlesSatisfaction \(\rightarrow\) productivity
MethodTime and motion studyPrinciples from experienceExperiments, observation
Informal groupIgnoredIgnoredCentral
ContributionStandards, incentives, efficiencyManagement process, 14 principlesMotivation, participation, human relations
LimitationMechanical, monotonyRigid, universal claimsNeglects structure, economics
Advantages of behavioural over scientific (78 Bh, 73 Shr)
  • Treats workers as humans, not machines.
  • Uses informal groups instead of ignoring them.
  • Participation raises commitment.
  • Lower turnover, absenteeism and conflict.
  • Quality improves with morale.
Advantages over modern theory (82 Ba)
  • Simpler to apply; needs no models or data.
  • Directly improves morale and motivation, where quantitative models ignore people.
  • Still the base of HR practice.
  • Admit that modern theory integrates it.

column1: Modern management theories: system approach and contingency approach
column4:
• After 1950; four streams:
    1. Quantitative: build a model expressing the system's effectiveness as a function of variables, at least one controllable. Tools: OR, maths, simulation, model building. Taylor's method was its early form. Systematizes managerial thinking.
    2. System: organization = open system of interrelated sub-systems; inputs (information, energy, materials) \(\rightarrow\) conversion (men-machine system) \(\rightarrow\) outputs + feedback, all steered by a plan (Boulding, Johnson, Rosenzweig, Churchman, late 1960s). System = “an established arrangement of components which leads to accomplishment of particular objectives as per plan”.
    3. Contingency: “it depends”.
    4. Operational: Koontz, O'Donnell, Weihrich: management is a universal body of knowledge for every level and enterprise, applied with judgement to each firm's real problems.
Characteristics of modern thought
  • System approach; dynamic; adaptive.
  • Multidisciplinary; multivariable in thought.
  • Multi-motivated in action.
  • Multi-level and multi-dimensional.
  • Probabilistic, not deterministic.
Contingency approach
  • Woodward, Fiedler, Lawrence and Lorsch.
  • No one best way: the right structure, style, technique depends on the situation (size, technology, environment, people).
  • Eg a routine garment line suits tight rules; an R&D lab suits loose, participative control.
Importance
  • Practical and flexible: fits the answer to the problem.
  • Integrates classical, behavioural and quantitative tools.
  • Fits fast-changing environments.
  • Trains managers to diagnose before acting.
  • Weakness: no firm principles, hard to teach.

• Peter Drucker (1954): superior and subordinate jointly set objectives, then review performance against them.

Merits

Demerits

  • Favours short-term, measurable goals over quality.

column1: Forms of ownership: list with brief explanation; choosing one; how an organization changes its form
column4:
• Firm = ownership unit combining men, materials, machines to produce and sell at a profit.
  • Five forms:
    1. Single ownership: one owner, unlimited liability.
    2. Partnership: 2+ partners by a deed, share profit and loss.
    3. Joint stock company: capital from shareholders, limited liability, separate legal entity.
    4. Cooperative society: voluntary, one member one vote, service motive.
    5. Public corporation: created by special act, owned by government.
Choosing a form: evaluation criteria
  • Size and nature of the business.
  • Capital: start-up and future needs.
  • Liability exposure: can the owners risk personal property?
  • Control the owners want to keep.
  • Tax consideration.
  • Managerial ability available.
  • Business goals and succession plans (continuity).
  • Cost of formation and government rules.
Changing form of ownership (73 Shr)
  • Growth needs capital and skills one owner lacks \(\rightarrow\) owner takes partners.
  • Partnership's unlimited liability and instability \(\rightarrow\) convert to a private limited company.
  • More capital needed \(\rightarrow\) public limited via IPO.
  • Reverse path: loss-making public enterprise \(\rightarrow\) privatized.
Nepali examples verified/added
  • Chaudhary Group: family trading shop \(\rightarrow\) group of companies \(\rightarrow\) listed CG / Nabil holdings.
  • Nepal Telecommunications Corporation \(\rightarrow\) Nepal Doorsanchar Company Ltd (2004) \(\rightarrow\) listed public company.
  • Bhrikuti Paper, Bansbari Leather: public enterprises privatized in the 1990s.

column1: Single ownership (sole proprietorship): features, advantages, limitations
column4:
Features
  • Oldest, simplest; one person owns, finances, manages, bears all risk.
  • Owner and business are the same in law.
  • Unlimited liability: personal property liable for business debts.
  • Suits small shops, cottage industry, handicrafts, farming.
Advantages
  • Easy and cheap to form and dissolve; few legal formalities.
  • Full control, prompt decisions, flexibility.
  • Direct motivation: all profit to owner.
  • Business secrecy.
  • Personal contact with customers and employees.
  • Little government control.
Limitations
  • Limited capital.
  • Limited managerial skill (one person cannot master production, marketing, finance, HR).
  • Unlimited liability.
  • Uncertain life: ends with owner's death or illness.
  • Cannot compete with large firms; no economies of scale.
  • Heavy workload, stress; isolation in decisions.

column1: Partnership: features, types of partners, advantages and difficulties
column4:
Features
  • Association of 2+ persons to run a business and share profit.
  • Formed by agreement: partnership deed (capital, profit ratio, duties, dissolution).
  • Unlimited, joint and several liability (except limited partners).
  • Mutual agency: each partner binds the firm.
  • No separate legal entity; restricted transfer of interest.
Types of partners
  • General / active: manage, unlimited liability.
  • Limited: liability up to capital; no say in management.
  • Sleeping / silent: capital only, no management, still liable.
  • Nominal: lends name only; no capital.
  • Minor: under 18, benefits only.
  • Partner by estoppel: implies being a partner, liable to third parties.
Advantages
  • Easy to form; little regulation.
  • More capital than sole owner.
  • Complementary skills; division of labour.
  • Shared risk; prompt decisions (few people).
  • Flexibility; personal interest of partners.
Difficulties / disadvantages
  • Unlimited liability of at least one partner.
  • Conflict, misunderstanding between partners \(\rightarrow\) instability.
  • Limited life: ends on death, insolvency, retirement of a partner.
  • Mutual agency: one partner's mistake binds all.
  • Cannot easily transfer share; capital still limited.
  • Unequal effort vs equal sharing breeds resentment.
  • Less secrecy than a sole owner; hard to dispose of one's interest.

column1: Joint stock company: meaning, characteristics, types, formation in Nepal, advantages and disadvantages
column2: 234568
column4:
• Meaning: voluntary association of persons, registered under the Companies Act, whose capital is divided into transferable shares. Shareholders own it; an elected board of directors manages it (elected at the AGM).
Characteristics
  • Created by law (registration); separate legal entity.
  • Perpetual succession: unaffected by death of shareholders.
  • Limited liability: up to share value.
  • Transferable shares (freely in public company).
  • Common seal; can sue and be sued.
  • Ownership separate from management.
  • Large membership, large capital.
Types (Companies Act 2063, Nepal) verified/added
  • Private limited: 1 to 101 shareholders; cannot invite the public to buy shares; share transfer restricted; name ends “Pvt. Ltd.”.
  • Public limited: min 7 promoters, no upper limit; min paid-up capital Rs 1 crore; shares offered to public and listed; “Ltd.”.
  • Adhikari's “max 50” for private is the old Indian figure; Nepal's is 101.
Formation / registration in Nepal verified/added
  1. Promotion: promoters identify the idea, feasibility, name.
  2. Name approval from the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) (online, ocr.gov.np).
  3. Documents filed:
    • Application form.
    • Memorandum of Association: name, objectives, registered office, authorized / issued / paid-up capital.
    • Articles of Association: internal rules, board, meetings, share transfer.
    • Promoters' citizenship (passport for foreigners); agreement among promoters; consent of directors.
    • Registration fee (scaled to authorized capital).
  4. OCR scrutinizes \(\rightarrow\) certificate of incorporation.
  5. PAN / VAT at Inland Revenue; local ward registration.
  6. Public company only: prospectus approved by SEBON, IPO, certificate of commencement of business, listing at NEPSE.
Advantages
  • Huge capital from many investors; fresh issue possible.
  • Limited liability \(\rightarrow\) attracts investors.
  • Transferable shares \(\rightarrow\) liquidity.
  • Stability, continuity.
  • Professional, efficient management.
  • Economies of large-scale production.
  • Public confidence (audited, published accounts); easy loans.
  • Social benefit: jobs, investment opportunity.
Disadvantages
  • Difficult, costly, lengthy formation; legal formalities.
  • Lack of personal interest (salaried managers, scattered owners).
  • Delay in decisions (board meetings).
  • Lack of secrecy.
  • Excessive government regulation.
  • Directors may exploit shareholders; speculation in shares; favouritism.
  • Impersonal labour relations.

  • Transferable shares: an owner can exit without closing the firm.
  • Professional management by an elected board.

column1: Co-operative societies: meaning, features, types, merits and demerits
column4:
• Meaning: voluntary association of persons on equal footing for common economic interest; service motive, not profit. Motto: “each for all and all for each”.
  • Features:
    • Voluntary, open membership.
    • Democratic management: one member one vote, regardless of shares.
    • Limited dividend; surplus shared as patronage bonus.
    • Self-help and equality.
    • Separate legal entity after registration.
  • Nepal: registered under the Cooperative Act 2074; a primary cooperative needs at least 30 members verified/added.
Merits
  • Easy formation; limited liability; continuity.
  • Democratic; protects weak members.
  • Eliminates middlemen \(\rightarrow\) cheaper goods, better prices.
  • Government support, tax concessions; reduces inequality.
Types
  1. Producers': small producers pool raw materials, tools, sell output (dairy, handicraft, cottage industry).
  2. Consumers': buy wholesale, sell daily goods to members cheaply.
  3. Marketing: farmers, artisans sell produce jointly (Eg milk cooperatives).
  4. Housing: members get land, build houses at low cost.
  5. Credit / savings and credit: pool savings, lend to members at fair rates (most common in Nepal).
  6. Multipurpose: several services together.
  7. Farming: small farmers pool land for mechanized farming.
Demerits
  • Limited capital; inefficient, amateur management.
  • Lack of motivation (fixed dividend); lack of secrecy.
  • Lack of co-ordination; members lose the spirit of co-operation over time.
  • Undue political influence, favouritism; misuse of funds (Nepal's savings-cooperative scandals).

Disadvantages
  • Political interference; appointments by politics, not merit.
  • Inefficiency, bureaucracy, losses (no profit pressure).
  • Monopoly \(\rightarrow\) poor service to customers.
  • Autonomy often only on paper; delay in decisions.

column1: Organization structure: meaning, factors, how it is designed for an enterprise
column4:
• Meaning: the framework that divides total activities into groups, fixes superior-subordinate relations and authority, and shows who reports to whom. Shown on an organization chart.
  • Covers division of labour, coordination, communication, workflow, formal power.
  • Depends on:
    • Size of the firm; nature of product.
    • Technology; complexity of problems.
    • Environment; competence of staff.
  • Types: line, functional, line & staff, committee, (matrix, project).
How it is designed (steps)
  1. Set objectives.
  2. Identify and list activities.
  3. Group activities into departments (by function, product, area, customer).
  4. Decide levels and span of control.
  5. Assign authority and responsibility; delegate.
  6. Set coordination and communication links.
  7. Draw the chart; review as the firm grows.
  • No single best structure: each firm evolves its own.
  • The structure is the skeleton: it divides total activity into groups, prescribes each person's authority, and so shows the hierarchy: persons arranged by rank.
  • An organization chart draws it: boxes = positions, lines = authority, dashed or side boxes = advisory (staff) bodies.
  • Read the chart right: the board sets policy, the GM executes it, an advisory committee advises the GM without commanding anyone.

column1: Line organization: features, advantages and disadvantages
column4:
• Oldest, simplest; also military or scalar organization.
  • Authority flows vertically top to bottom; responsibility bottom to top.
  • Each head has full control of his department (finance, production, sales); each department is subdivided into sections and is a self-supporting unit.
  • Lines of authority clearly defined; managers must be all-rounders.
  • Suits small firms, routine work, few employees.

Simple, easily understoodOverload on top executives
Clear authority and responsibilityNo specialization
Strong disciplineDictatorial, one-man show
Unity of commandDepends on a few key persons
Quick decisionsDuplication of work across departments
Rapid communication, easy coordinationUnsuitable for large firms
EconomicalScope for favouritism; poor communication upward
Each department self-supportingUndue reliance on key men; wastage of materials
Line organization: a single vertical chain from managing director to foremen.

column1: Functional organization: features, advantages and disadvantages (with sketch)
column4:
• Proposed by F.W. Taylor: all-round foremen were hard to find.
  • Work divided by function; each function under a specialist who commands workers only in his field.
  • Taylor's functional foremanship: 8 foremen.
    • Planning room (4): route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian.
    • Shop floor (4): gang boss, speed boss, repair boss, inspector.
  • Worker receives orders from several bosses \(\rightarrow\) breaks unity of command.
Functional structure: marketing, engineering, finance, production, each under its expert.
AdvantagesDisadvantages
Specialization, expert guidanceViolates unity of command \(\rightarrow\) indiscipline
Efficiency, standardized operationsOverlapping authority, conflicts
Easy selection and training of specialistsShifting of responsibility
Reduced burden on top executivesPoor coordination between functions
Lower cost through expertise; scope for growthDelayed decisions needing several experts; costly
Separation of planning from doing; lower prime costKills workers' initiative

column1: Line and staff organization; its advantages over line and functional organization
column4:
• Line structure \(+\) staff specialists (legal adviser, personnel, research, quality control) who advise line managers but have no command authority.
  • “Staff are thinkers, line are doers.”
  • Suits large plants: steel mills, electricity boards, big factories.
  • Why staff exist: line heads are busy with routine production, so staff do the investigation, research, recording and advising, and supply expert information.
General advantages
  • Specialized knowledge available; suits progressive, growing business.
  • Less wastage, improved quality, better decisions.
Advantages over line organization
  • Expert advice \(\rightarrow\) better decisions.
  • Relieves overloaded line executives.
  • Suits growth and complexity.
Advantages over functional organization
  • Keeps unity of command and discipline.
  • No overlapping authority.
  • Clear accountability for results.
Line and staff: dashed lines are staff (advice only).
Disadvantages
  • Line-staff friction; line resents advice.
  • Staff without authority may be ineffective.
  • Staff not accountable for results \(\rightarrow\) lethargy.
  • Expensive; confusion over duties.
  • Line may lose initiative, over-rely on staff.
  • Chances of misinterpreting staff advice.

column1: Committee organization: types, merits and demerits
column4:
• Formal group of 2+ persons appointed to deliberate on problems one person cannot solve; members meet, discuss, recommend or decide.
  • Not a separate structure: added to line or line & staff at any level.
Types
  • Ad hoc: temporary, dissolves after its task.
  • Standing / permanent: repetitive work (purchase, research committee).
  • Advisory (staff): recommend only.
  • Executive (line): has power to decide and enforce.
  • Formal / informal: by charter or by convenience.
Merits
  • Pooled knowledge; problem seen from several views.
  • Coordination between departments.
  • Democratic, participative; better acceptance.
  • New ideas; checks concentration of power.
Demerits
  • Slow decisions; costly (many people's time).
  • Compromise, not the best decision; non-uniform final decisions.
  • Divided responsibility (no one accountable).
  • Dominated by a few members.

column1: Matrix / project organization; which structure suits a (temporary) engineering project?
column4:
• Project organization: a temporary team under a project manager, formed for one project, dissolved at completion.
  • Matrix: project structure laid over a functional one; staff report to a functional manager (technical) and a project manager (schedule, cost). Two bosses. (Figure in \(\S\)1.4.)
  • Merits:
    • Efficient use of specialists across projects.
    • Clear project accountability.
    • Skill development, job rotation.
    • Fast response to clients.
  • Demerits:
    • Violates unity of command (two bosses).
    • Power struggle between functional and project managers.
    • Complex, confusing; costly coordination.
Best for a temporary engineering project: project / matrix
  • Project has fixed start, end, budget, scope: a dedicated project manager owns all three.
  • Needs many disciplines (civil, electrical, mechanical, finance) together.
  • Team disbands at completion; specialists return to departments.
  • Single point of contact for client; faster decisions than line.
  • Line would lack specialists, functional would scatter responsibility, committees are too slow.
  • Large one-off project (hydropower, highway) \(\rightarrow\) pure project organization; firm running many projects \(\rightarrow\) matrix.

column1: Authority and responsibility; span of control; policy group vs executive group
column4:
Authority vs responsibility
BasisAuthorityResponsibility
MeaningRight to decide, command, use resourcesObligation to perform assigned work
FlowDownwardUpward
DelegationCan be delegatedCannot be delegated fully
SourcePosition (formal)Superior-subordinate relation
 Principle: authority must be equal to responsibility.
Policy group vs executive group
  • Policy group: board of directors / top management; frames objectives, policies, budgets (administration, thinking).
  • Executive group: managers who carry policies out, direct day-to-day work (management, doing).
Span of control
  • No. of subordinates directly reporting to one superior.
  • Narrow span: close supervision, many levels, tall structure, slow communication.
  • Wide span: flat structure, fast communication, more delegation, less control.
  • Typical: 5–6 at top, 15–20 at shop floor.
  • In a line organization span decides the no. of levels.
  • Factors deciding the span:
    • Ability of the manager and of subordinates.
    • Nature of work: routine \(\rightarrow\) wide; complex \(\rightarrow\) narrow.
    • Degree of delegation.
    • Communication tools.
    • Geographic spread of subordinates.
  • Graicunas: with \(n\) subordinates the relationships to manage are \(n\,(2^{n-1} + n - 1)\): 6 people \(\rightarrow\) 222. Why span must stay limited.
  • For \(n\) = 1 to 8: 1, 6, 18, 44, 100, 222, 490, 1080. Adding the 7th subordinate more than doubles the load.
Narrow span (2 to 3 each): tall, 3 levels, close supervision.
Wide span (8): flat, 2 levels, more delegation.

column1: Purchasing: meaning, objectives (5 R's), principles, functions of the purchasing department
column4:
• Purchasing: acquiring materials, supplies, machines, tools and services by payment, for the firm's operation. First phase of materials management.
  • Alford and Beatty: “procuring of materials, supplies, machines, tools and services required for equipment, maintenance and operation of a manufacturing plant.”
  • Objectives: the 5 R's: right quality, right quantity, right price, right time, right source (+ right place).
  • Continuous supply, minimum inventory, good vendor relations, low total cost.
Principles of purchasing
  • Buy to specification and standards.
  • Competitive quotations; buy on total value, not lowest price.
  • Centralized purchasing for economy.
  • Ethical dealing, no favouritism; prompt payment.
  • Develop reliable, alternative sources.
  • Keep records; review make-or-buy.
Purchasing vs procurement (71 Ch)
  • Purchasing: the buying transaction (order, pay).
  • Procurement: wider: need identification, sourcing, contracts, buying, logistics, receiving, vendor management; includes lease, hire, transfer.
Functions of purchasing department
  1. Receive and check purchase requisitions.
  2. Review specifications; standardize, simplify.
  3. Keep records of materials, substitutes, suppliers, prices.
  4. Call and analyse quotations; select vendor.
  5. Negotiate; place orders; follow up.
  6. Inspect: right quality and quantity.
  7. Prepare purchase budget.
  8. Buy at right time and economical rate.
  9. Keep uninterrupted supply to production.
  10. Liaison between vendors and production, QC, finance, stores.
  11. Ensure prompt payment \(\rightarrow\) good vendor relations.
  12. Develop new sources; handle sub-contracts.
  13. Keep inventory optimum; dispose of scrap and salvage.
Role of purchasing and marketing departments
  • Purchasing: input side, supplies right materials at lowest total cost \(\rightarrow\) cost and quality of product.
  • Marketing: output side, finds needs, sells product, brings revenue.
  • Together they link the firm to suppliers and customers.

column1: Methods of purchasing; purchasing procedure (process outline)
column4:
Methods (choice depends on firm size, nature and quantity of material)
  1. By requirement (hand-to-mouth): buy whenever the need arises.
  2. For a specified period: regular standard items (oils, coolants, stationery) bought for a future period set by production schedules.
  3. Market purchasing: requirements from production planning + market trends \(\rightarrow\) buy ahead of need when prices are low and likely to rise.
  4. Speculative: buy excess at a price low for profit; price trend, not need, decides (unlike market purchasing).
  5. Rate contract: suppliers supply at agreed prices for 2–3 years, reviewable on notice; basic materials (pig iron, steel, coal, coke).
  6. Group purchasing: items bought in groups or lots in one order, not one order per item.
  7. Through a government supplies agency (India's DGS&D): agency fixes annual rate contracts; departments order directly at those rates; firms certify they sell no cheaper elsewhere.
By procedure (AJ Sir)
  • Direct: urgent, from a known supplier.
  • Quotation: at least 3 quotations, pick best.
  • Tender: public notice in newspapers; sealed bids; evaluate (large or public purchases; Public Procurement Act 2063 in Nepal).
Purchasing procedure (draw this for “outline of the purchasing process”, 76 Ash)
  • Purchase order copies go to stores, accounts and the requesting department.
  • Inspection ends in a goods-received report; only then is the invoice passed for payment.

column1: Marketing: definition, concept, and its importance (in modern business and the digital era)
column4:
• Stanton: “a total system of interacting business activities designed to plan, price, promote and distribute want-satisfying products and services to present and potential customers.”
  • Kotler: satisfying needs and wants through exchange processes.
  • Flow view: business activities that direct the flow of goods and services from producer to consumer: the right product, right place, right quantity, right price, right time.
  • Starts with identifying a consumer need, ends with satisfying it; the modern concept stresses consumer needs and freedom to choose.
  • 4 P's (marketing mix): product, price, place, promotion.
Marketing concept
  • Evolution: production \(\rightarrow\) product \(\rightarrow\) selling \(\rightarrow\) marketing \(\rightarrow\) societal concept.
  • Three pillars: customer orientation, profit through satisfaction (not volume), integrated effort of all departments.
  • Selling concept: “sell what we make”. Marketing concept: “make what customers want”.
Marketing research (4 elements)
  • Current sales analysis: what sells, where, to whom.
  • Market intelligence: competitors' moves.
  • Market analysis: reaction to price changes and new products.
  • Product evaluation: how the product performs for users.
Importance
  • To the firm:
    • Brings revenue, the only source of profit.
    • Tells production what to make.
    • Builds brand and loyalty; survives competition.
  • To consumers:
    • Right product, right place, right price.
    • Wider choice and product information.
  • To society / economy:
    • Creates demand \(\rightarrow\) production \(\rightarrow\) jobs.
    • Raises living standard.
    • Distribution to remote areas; exports earn foreign exchange.
  • Fundamental: without a customer nothing else in the firm is needed (Drucker: “marketing and innovation are the two basic functions”).
Importance in the digital era (81 Ba)
  • Social media, search, e-commerce: reach millions at low cost.
  • Data analytics: precise targeting, personalization.
  • Measurable ROI; real-time campaigns.
  • Two-way engagement, reviews, influencers build trust.
  • Small firms and startups compete globally.
  • Digital payments (eSewa, Khalti) enable online selling in Nepal.

column1: Functions of marketing
column4:
Classical grouping (Adhikari): marketing adds value through its functions
  1. Exchange (ownership transfer):
    • Buying: assembling goods for resale or use.
    • Selling: finding buyers, persuading, transferring ownership.
  2. Physical distribution:
    • Transport: moves goods to where they are needed (place utility).
    • Storage / warehousing: holds goods until needed (time utility).
  3. Facilitating:
    • Standardization and grading: uniform quality, easy buying.
    • Financing: credit to dealers and customers.
    • Risk bearing: price fall, spoilage, theft; insurance.
    • Market information: demand, prices, competitors.
Modern list (AJ Sir)
  • Product / service management: what to make, features, quality.
  • Pricing: cost, competition, demand.
  • Promotion: advertising, sales promotion, publicity.
  • Distribution (channel): wholesalers, retailers, online.
  • Selling and financing.
  • Market information management, buying.
  • Packaging and branding: protects and identifies the product.
  • After-sales service: installation, repair, warranty.

column1: Advertising: definition, and why it is one of the best forms of marketing
column4:
• Definition: paid, non-personal communication of information about a product, service or idea through mass media by an identified sponsor, to create or maintain demand.
    • Media: newspaper, TV, radio, online, billboards.
    • From Latin ad verto, “to turn towards”: turning attention toward the product.
  • Integral part of marketing; the pivot of modern trade: informs customers what and where, creates demand.
  • Real goal: effective communication that modifies attitudes or behaviour of the receiver.
  • Why the best form:
    • Mass reach at low cost per contact; repetition builds memory.
    • Creates awareness and new demand; launches new products.
    • Builds brand image and goodwill; supports salesmen and dealers.
    • Informs and educates consumers; counters competition.
    • Digital ads are targeted and measurable.

column1: Salesmanship; marketing vs purchasing; marketing software products in Nepal
column4:
Salesmanship is an important ingredient of marketing? Agree (73 Shr)
  • Personal selling persuades face to face, explains technical products, handles objections, closes the sale.
  • Brings customer feedback to the firm; builds relationships.
  • But it is one ingredient: product, price, place and research come first.
Marketing vs purchasing (68 Ch)
  • Purchasing: inputs, firm is buyer, aims at low cost, deals with suppliers.
  • Marketing: outputs, firm is seller, aims at revenue and satisfaction, deals with customers.
Challenges for marketing software in Nepal (76 Ash)
  • Small domestic market; low willingness to pay for software.
  • Piracy; free alternatives.
  • Preference for foreign brands; trust deficit in local products.
  • Low digital literacy and internet access outside cities.
  • Limits on international payments; weak IP law enforcement.
  • Skilled marketers scarce; brain drain.
  • Response: freemium, local language, SaaS subscriptions, export markets, partnerships with banks and telecoms.

column1: Define personnel management. Explain its functions and its role in the organization
column2: 123458
column4:
• Flippo: “the planning, organizing, directing and controlling of the procurement, development, compensation, integration and maintenance of personnel, to accomplish organizational, individual and social goals.”
  • Simple: the part of management that obtains, develops, uses and keeps a satisfied workforce. Also called human resource management.
  • Three-part view: the part of management dealing with human resources:
    • their procurement;
    • their development in skills, knowledge, attitude;
    • their motivation toward objectives, by keeping a climate that favours such development.
Aims
  • Get the best out of people.
  • Maximum individual development.
  • Better service to society.
  • Good labour relations.
Three aspects (AJ Sir)
  • Welfare: working conditions, canteen, housing, health, safety.
  • Labour / personnel: recruitment, pay, promotion, training.
  • Industrial relations: unions, disputes, collective bargaining.
Characteristics
  1. Part of general management.
  2. Has its own principles and policies.
  3. Humanistic: deals with people, not things.
  4. A philosophy of management: how the firm treats its people.
  5. Carries advisory, executive and administrative responsibilities.
Managerial functions
  • Planning: manpower needs, policies, programmes.
  • Organizing: structure of the HR department, tasks.
  • Directing: motivating, guiding employees.
  • Coordinating and controlling: audit of HR results against plan.
Role in the organization
  • Supplies the right people at the right time.
  • Builds skills (training) \(\rightarrow\) productivity.
  • Fair pay, incentives \(\rightarrow\) motivation, low turnover.
  • Industrial peace: handles grievances, unions.
  • Welfare and safety \(\rightarrow\) morale, fewer accidents.
  • Advises line managers; keeps records; ensures labour-law compliance (Labour Act 2074 in Nepal).
  • Aligns people with strategy \(\rightarrow\) growth and development of the firm.
Operative functions
  1. Procurement: manpower planning, job analysis, recruitment, selection, placement, induction.
  2. Development: training, executive development, career planning, promotion.
  3. Compensation: job evaluation, wage and salary administration, incentives.
  4. Integration: reconcile employee and organizational interests: communication, grievance handling, collective bargaining.
  5. Maintenance: health, safety, welfare, social security, ergonomics.
  6. Motivation: monetary and non-monetary incentives.
  7. Records and separation: personnel records, transfers, retirement, exit.
Adhikari's list of functions (write it for “functions” at 5 marks)
  1. Develop personnel policy.
  2. Manpower planning.
  3. Recruitment and selection.
  4. Analysis, description and valuation of work.
  5. Compensation and appraisal schemes.
  6. Personnel records.
  7. Welfare and safety programmes.
  8. Training and development.
  9. Wage and salary administration.
  10. Collective bargaining with unions.
  11. Promotion, transfer, retirement.
Principles of personnel management
  1. Scientific selection: right person for the right job.
  2. Fair reward: pay matched to work and market.
  3. High morale: satisfied, willing workers.
  4. Dignity of labour: respect every job.
  5. Team spirit among employees.
  6. Effective communication both ways.
  7. Joint management: workers consulted on decisions affecting them.
  8. Effective utilization of each person's ability.
  9. Maximum individual development.
  10. National prosperity through productive industry.

column1: Personnel policy: what it must include, its importance, and why it is discussed with new employees
column4:
• Personnel policy (employee handbook): written statement of what the employer expects from employees and what they may expect in return. A guide for quick, consistent decisions; a means to an end, not an objective.
  • Eg a “promotion from within” policy serves the objective of employee development.
  • Objectives: maximum development and use of workers' abilities; good labour relations; protect interests of labour and customers.
Terms a good personnel policy includes
  1. Welcome message; company name, history, values, objectives, structure.
  2. Recruitment and selection: sources, procedure, probation.
  3. Working hours, attendance, leave (sick, annual, holidays).
  4. Pay: salary structure, allowances, overtime, incentives, bonus.
  5. Benefits: insurance, provident fund, gratuity, pension, education aid.
  6. Training and development; promotion and transfer policy.
  7. Code of conduct: discipline, dress, harassment, conflict of interest.
  8. Health and safety; accident procedure.
  9. Grievance procedure; union and collective bargaining.
  10. Separation: resignation notice, retirement, dismissal, exit process.
Importance
  • Consistency and fairness: same rule for everyone \(\rightarrow\) trust.
  • Quick decisions by managers without referring upward.
  • Reduces conflict and grievances; legal protection for both sides.
  • Attracts and retains good staff; builds culture.
Why discuss it at hiring / with new employees
  • Employee knows rights and duties from day one: pay, leave, benefits, discipline.
  • No surprises later \(\rightarrow\) fewer disputes, lower early turnover.
  • Part of induction: faster adjustment, sense of belonging.
  • Written acknowledgement protects the employer legally.
  • Clarifies expectations on conduct, safety, harassment.

column1: Manpower (human resource) planning: meaning, steps, and why it is needed
column4:
• Definition: the process of having the right number of the right kind of people at the right place and right time, doing the jobs they suit. Formally: “the scientific process of allocating the right quantity of right men required in future at right time on the right job”.
  • Manpower = total skills, knowledge, talent, creativity and values of the workforce.
  • Two objectives: use present employees fully; fill future needs.
  • Types: macro (national) vs micro (firm); short, medium, long term.
  • Factors affecting the estimate:
    • Working hours and shifts.
    • Nature of production and product mix.
    • Performance rate of workers.
    • Hours lost to absenteeism; labour turnover.
Steps of the HR planning process
Importance / need
  • No shortage, no surplus: avoids idle labour and overload.
  • Cuts labour cost; right people raise productivity.
  • Anticipates retirement, turnover, expansion: vacancies filled in time.
  • Basis for recruitment, training, career planning.
  • Copes with technological change: new skills planned ahead.
  • Attracts talent; supports succession planning.
  • Nepal: high outmigration of skilled youth \(\rightarrow\) planning replacements and retention is essential.
Notes on the steps (left)
  • Demand depends on workload, expansion, technology, budget.
  • Supply: internal (promotion, transfer, retirement, turnover) and external (labour market).
  • Net requirement = demand \(-\) supply: shortage \(\rightarrow\) recruit or train; surplus \(\rightarrow\) redeploy or downsize.
Adhikari's version of the steps
  1. Understand the business activities.
  2. Identify the tasks.
  3. Forecast manpower.
  4. Job analysis.
  5. Review existing manpower.
  6. Anticipate supply from outside.
  7. Manpower management (act on the gap).

column1: Explain the process of recruitment and selection of manpower (steps of hiring); scientific selection
column4:
• Recruitment: searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply; creates a pool (positive process). Dale S. Beach: “the development and maintenance of adequate manpower resources. It involves the creation of a pool of available labor upon whom the organization can depend when it needs additional employees.”
  • Selection: choosing the most suitable from the pool by eliminating the rest (negative process).
  • Hiring: the final act of appointing, with offer, contract, placement.
Steps of recruitment and selection
Notes on the steps
  • Before step 1: job analysis, job description and a staff requisition fix what is needed; the vacancy is advertised (title, duties, qualification, deadline).
  • Screening and preliminary interview drop the plainly unfit early and cheaply.
  • Employment tests: intelligence, trade, psychological, aptitude, interest, personality.
  • Employment interview: HR first, then the department head.
  • Reference check: former employers, teachers; background verification.
  • Final selection: offer letter, appointment, contract.
  • Placement and induction: orientation, handbook (add these when the question says “steps of hiring”).
  • Each step eliminates: selection is a series of hurdles, which is why it is called a negative process.
Sources of recruitment
  • Internal: promotion, transfer, internal posting, former employees, employee referrals.
  • External: advertisement (newspaper, websites like merojob, LinkedIn), campus recruitment, employment agencies, walk-ins, unions, consultants.
Scientific selection
  • Taylor's principle: right person for the right job, one who maintains the output with least effort.
  • Selection by objective tests and standards, not favour or guess.
  • Methods: psychological and aptitude tests, trade tests, structured interviews, work samples, assessment centres, medical tests.
Fitness factors checked
  • Physical: sound body, limbs, height, weight, eyesight.
  • Personal: age, sex, marital status, experience, family.
  • Proficiency: skill and ability now: the basic fit.
  • Competency: potential to learn and become proficient.
  • Temperament, character; vocational interest.
Recruitment vs selection vs hiring
BasisRecruitmentSelection / hiring
AimAttract many applicantsPick the best, appoint
NaturePositiveNegative (eliminating)
OrderFirstAfter recruitment
OutputPool of candidatesEmployee with contract

column1: Outsourcing
column4:
• Contracting a function to an outside firm instead of hiring staff for it.
  • Eg security, cleaning, payroll, IT support, call centres; Nepal's IT firms do outsourced work for foreign clients.
  • In recruitment: an agency does the hiring, or staff are supplied by a manpower company.
Advantages
  • Lower cost: no salaries, benefits, training for that function.
  • Specialist skill and technology of the vendor.
  • Management focuses on core work.
  • Flexible headcount: scale up or down by contract.
Disadvantages
  • Less control over quality and timing.
  • Confidentiality and data risk.
  • Dependence on one vendor.
  • Staff morale falls if jobs are cut.

column1: Referral recruitment: pros and cons
column4:

Pros

  • Closes the door to better outside talent.
  • Use it with the same tests and interviews as other candidates.
