column1: Training and development: meaning, need, methods, and how training needs are identified
column4:
• Training: planned learning of specific knowledge and skills to do the present job better; short term; mainly for workers.
  • Development: long-term education for future roles, conceptual and managerial growth; mainly for executives.
  • Training, formally: “a well thought and well planned process of conscious learning of new knowledge and skills for improving the learner's ability to perform certain tasks more efficiently and effectively, in the immediate or near future, with active support of some other individuals.”
  • Development, formally: long-term, systematic process by which managers gain conceptual and theoretical knowledge; an executive development programme raises their capability to achieve objectives.
  • Objectives: disseminate knowledge, develop skills, change attitudes.
Need / role (esp. for new employees)
  • New hires become productive in the minimum time; no learning by mistakes.
  • Higher productivity, quality; less wastage and spoilage.
  • Fewer accidents, less machine breakdown.
  • Less supervision needed.
  • Morale, job satisfaction; lower turnover and absenteeism.
  • Keeps pace with new technology; flexibility.
  • Career growth, higher earnings; builds future managers.
Identifying training needs
  • Organization analysis: goals, problems (low output, high scrap, accidents).
  • Task analysis: job description vs skills required.
  • Person analysis: performance appraisal gaps, supervisor reports, self-assessment.
  • Other signals: complaints, new machines, promotions, surveys, exit interviews.
Methods: workers
  • Demonstration: instructor actually shows how to do the task; small shops, auto repair workshops (Eg how to do a job on a centre lathe).
  • On-the-job: supervisor instructs a new worker at the machine: nature of work, tools, safety; shows how an experienced worker does it. Most realistic.
  • Vestibule: a separate training school duplicating, as nearly as possible, the real equipment, materials and conditions; many trainees, no production pressure; costly.
  • Apprenticeship: long, for all-round craftsmen (machinists, tool makers, millwrights, fitters, welders); best for large firms with steady demand for skill.
  • Special courses: knowledge-based, in-house or outside institutes.
Methods: supervisors
  • Induction and orientation.
  • Lecture (classroom); conference.
  • Written instruction.
  • Training within industry (TWI).
Methods: executives
  • On the job:
    • Understudy (appointed assistant to a manager).
    • Committee membership; job rotation.
    • Job enlargement / enrichment; MBO.
  • Off the job: lectures, case study, business games, role playing, seminars, e-learning.

column1: HR problems: talent poaching; short-term employee development programme; appropriate vs inappropriate human resources
column4:
Tackling talent poaching (79 Ba)
  • Competitive pay, reviewed against the market.
  • Retention bonus, ESOP, bond or notice clauses.
  • Clear career path, promotion from within.
  • Training, recognition, good culture, flexible work.
  • Stay interviews; fix reasons found in exit interviews.
  • Succession planning so no one person is critical.
Short-term development programme
  1. Identify skill gaps (appraisal).
  2. Set 3–6 month objectives per employee.
  3. Workshops, mentoring, job rotation, online courses.
  4. Review, reward, plan the next cycle.
Appropriate vs inappropriate human resources (73 Shr)
  • Appropriate: people whose skills, qualification, attitude and number match job requirements \(\rightarrow\) productive, satisfied.
  • Inappropriate: a mismatch.
    • Over-qualified: bored, leave soon.
    • Under-qualified: errors, need close supervision.
    • Surplus: idle cost.
    • Wrong attitude: conflict, low morale.
  • Ideas to get appropriate HR:
    • Manpower planning and job analysis.
    • Scientific selection.
    • Training and appraisal.
    • Redeployment of surplus staff.
    • Fair pay to keep the right people.

column1: Job analysis: meaning, methods, job description and job specification
column4:
• Job: group of tasks, duties and responsibilities done by one person for pay.
  • Job analysis: systematic study of a job to find its tasks and the skills, knowledge, abilities and responsibilities needed to do it well. Answers what, how, why, with what tools, under what conditions.
  • Outputs: job description (about the job) and job specification (about the person). Used for recruitment, training, job evaluation, pay, appraisal.
Data collected in a job analysis
  1. Job identification.
  2. Nature of the job: major and other duties.
  3. Operations performed.
  4. Materials and equipment used.
  5. Skill: education, training, responsibility, job knowledge, mental capability, accuracy \(\rightarrow\) degree of difficulty.
  6. Physical demands: activities, working conditions, hazards \(\rightarrow\) effort.
  7. Relation with other jobs.
  • Job: a regular assignment to one employee, with duties, responsibilities and conditions different from other assignments.
  • The analyst (or a trained supervisor) collects information, prepares the description, then works up the specification.
Job analysis yields the job description and job specification, and each feeds HR decisions.
Steps
  1. Collect background info (charts, old descriptions).
  2. Select jobs to analyse.
  3. Collect job data (methods below).
  4. Process and verify with job holder and supervisor.
  5. Prepare job description.
  6. Prepare job specification.
Methods of collecting data
  • Questionnaire: holders fill structured forms; cheap for many jobs; misunderstanding possible.
  • Interview: holder describes duties, even unobservable ones; may exaggerate.
  • Observation: analyst watches the work; firsthand; best for manual jobs; workers may change behaviour.
  • Diary / log, critical incident, technical conference with experts.
Most suitable in Nepal? (82 Bh)
  • Interview + observation:
    • Many small firms have no written records.
    • Jobs are manual or mixed, easy to watch.
    • Literacy varies \(\rightarrow\) questionnaires return poor data.
  • Large firms and banks can add questionnaires.
Job description (what the job is): identification, summary, work performed
  • Job title, code, department, location.
  • Job summary (purpose).
  • Duties and responsibilities: what, how, why.
  • Reporting relationships.
  • Machines, tools, materials.
  • Working conditions: shifts, hazards.
  • Pay grade, benefits.
Job specification (who can do it)
  • Education, training, experience.
  • Skills, knowledge, abilities.
  • Physical and mental requirements.
  • Personal qualities (communication, attitude).
Example: Lecturer, engineering college (81 Ba)
  • JD: title Lecturer, Dept of Electronics; reports to HoD.
    • Teach 16–18 periods/week; prepare lessons.
    • Supervise labs; set and evaluate exams.
    • Guide projects; research and publish; departmental duties.
  • JS:
    • Master's in relevant engineering, first division; NEC registration.
    • Teaching or industry experience preferred.
    • Communication and presentation skill, lab skills, ethics, research aptitude.
Job design (short note)
  • Structuring tasks of a job for productivity and satisfaction:
    • Simplification: narrow, easy tasks.
    • Rotation: move between jobs.
    • Enlargement: more tasks at the same level.
    • Enrichment: more responsibility and control.
    • Ergonomics: fit the job to the body.

column1: Job evaluation: meaning, methods, and comparison with merit rating
column4:
• Systematic determination of the relative worth of a job compared with others \(\rightarrow\) fair, uniform wage structure.
  • Principles:
    • Rate the job, not the man.
    • Uniformity of understanding of the factors.
    • Co-operation from employees.
  • War Manpower Commission (USA): an accurate job study answers four questions: what does the worker do? how? why? what skill does it take?
  • Non-quantitative methods:
    • Ranking: jobs ranked whole, most to least important; each head ranks his department's jobs, a central committee merges them into grades.
    • Classification / grading: jobs slotted into predefined grades.
  • Quantitative methods:
    • Factor comparison: skill, mental effort, physical effort, responsibility, working conditions compared factor by factor with key jobs.
    • Point rating: points per factor degree, totals set the grade.
BasisJob evaluationMerit rating
RatesThe jobThe person doing it
PurposeWage structure for the jobReward, promotion over the base wage
TimingBefore hiring, on job changePeriodically, after hiring
BasisJob analysisActual performance, traits
OutputJob gradesRanking of employees
Uses of job evaluation
  • Fair, consistent wage structure; removes pay anomalies.
  • Fewer wage disputes and grievances.
  • Basis for wage negotiation with unions.
  • Helps place new jobs into existing grades.

column1: Merit rating / performance appraisal: meaning, need, traditional and modern methods
column4:
• Merit rating: systematic, periodic assessment of an employee's worth in terms of job performance, integrity, leadership, behaviour, aptitude.
  • Factors: quality and quantity of work, job knowledge, dependability, attitude, initiative, versatility, leadership.
Why necessary
  • Basis for promotion, transfer, pay rise, bonus.
  • Feedback to employee \(\rightarrow\) improvement.
  • Identifies training needs.
  • Validates selection; objective, fair decisions; motivation.
Traditional methods (trait-based)
  • Ranking: best to worst, overall.
  • Paired / person-to-person comparison: each with every other.
  • Man-to-man comparison: against key men on 5 traits (physical qualities, personal qualities, intelligence, general value to service, leadership), 5 degrees each.
  • Grading: predefined grades (outstanding, satisfactory, unsatisfactory).
  • Graphic rating scale: traits rated on a scale; most common.
  • Checklist: yes/no statements.
  • Free essay: supervisor's written description.
  • Critical incident: record of good and bad events.
Modern methods (result-based)
  • MBO / appraisal by results: manager and employee jointly set goals, appraise against them.
  • Assessment centre: simulations, group exercises, in-basket tasks observed by trained assessors; for promotion.
  • 360-degree feedback: from superiors, peers, subordinates, customers, self. verified/added
  • BARS (behaviourally anchored rating scale): scale points tied to real behaviours. verified/added
  • Human resource accounting: employee's value in money. verified/added
  • KPI / balanced scorecard dashboards. verified/added
Merits of modern methods
  • Objective, measurable; less bias.
  • Employee participates \(\rightarrow\) commitment.
  • Links appraisal to goals and development.
360-degree feedback: ratings from every side of the employee.

column1: Wages and salary: difference, factors affecting the wage/salary structure, how wages are calculated, salary and benefits you expect
column4:
• Wage: remuneration for labour, paid per hour, day, week or per unit of output; production and manual workers.
  • Salary: fixed monthly or annual pay; office, professional, managerial staff.
  • Nominal (money) wage: cash only. Real wage: what the cash buys, plus benefits.
  • A wage should meet ordinary needs, give some comforts, and keep the worker's standard of living.
  • Structure:
    • Job classes / grades from job evaluation.
    • Flat rate or rate range per grade.
    • Direct pay: basic, overtime, bonus.
    • Indirect pay: insurance, provident fund, gratuity, allowances.
Three layers of wages
Minimum wage is the legal floor (Nepal revises it periodically).
Salary and benefits I would expect (82 Ba, 75 Ch)
  • Basic salary at or above market rate for the post, with annual increment.
  • Allowances: dearness, transport, communication, festival (Dashain) allowance.
  • Provident fund, gratuity / SSF contribution; health and accident insurance.
  • Paid leave; overtime; performance bonus.
  • Training, career growth; flexible hours. Justify with qualification and market data.
Factors affecting wage / salary structure
  1. Ability of the firm to pay (profit, size).
  2. Demand and supply of labour.
  3. Prevailing market rate for comparable jobs.
  4. Cost of living (inflation index).
  5. Legal provisions: minimum wage, Labour Act, SSF.
  6. Job requirements from job evaluation: skill, effort, responsibility, hazards.
  7. Productivity (output per man-hour).
  8. Bargaining power of trade unions.
  9. Employee's qualification, experience, seniority.
  10. Regularity of employment, working hours, promotion prospects, training cost.
Examples (80 Bh)
  • Supply-demand, market rate: an IT engineer in Kathmandu earns more than a same-degree engineer in a small town.
  • Legal: garment workers' pay rises when the government revises the minimum wage.
  • Bargaining power: a union-negotiated increase at NEA.
  • Cost of living: dearness allowance raised after inflation.

column1: Incentives: meaning, need, types
column4:
• Incentive: payment or benefit over and above normal wage, linked to output or performance above a standard, to motivate higher productivity.
  • Incentive scheme: a system of wage payment in which the earnings of an employee, a group, or all employees are directly related to output of acceptable quality above a standard, by a predetermined formula.
Why needed
  • Raises productivity, lowers unit cost.
  • Rewards efficient workers fairly.
  • Motivation, morale, job satisfaction.
  • Reduces supervision, absenteeism, turnover.
  • Attracts and retains talent.
Types
  • Financial: bonus, profit sharing, commission, piece-rate premium, ESOP.
  • Non-financial: praise, recognition, promotion, job security, training, flexible hours, better conditions.
  • Semi-financial: subsidized lunch, medical, recreation, pension.
  • Individual: based on one person's output (Taylor, Halsey, Rowan).
  • Group: based on team or plant output (Scanlon, Priestman, profit sharing): efficient workers help slow ones.

column1: How wages are calculated: wage plans and incentive formulas
column4:
Basic plans
  • Time rate: wage \(= T_a \times R\) (hours worked \(\times\) hourly rate). Simple, secure; no push for output.
  • Piece rate: wage \(=\) units \(\times\) rate per unit. Rewards output; no security.
  • Combined: guaranteed time wage + piece earnings above it.
Taylor's differential piece rate
  • By F.W. Taylor: rewards efficient workers, penalizes sluggish ones.
  • Two rates: low (Eg 80%) below standard, high (Eg 120%) at or above.
  • Example: standard 80 jobs/day (8 h), Rs 12/h \(\rightarrow\) standard rate \(12/10 =\) Rs 1.20.
    • A makes 75: \(75 \times 0.96 =\) Rs 72.
    • B makes 85: \(85 \times 1.44 =\) Rs 122.40.
Halsey premium plan (1891)
  • By Frederick A. Halsey, American engineer.
  • Minimum wage guaranteed; standard time fixed per job.
  • Time saved earns a fixed share (usually 50%) as bonus.
  • Bonus \(= \tfrac12 R\,(T_s - T_a)\); wage \(= T_a R + \tfrac12 R\,(T_s - T_a)\).
  • \(T_s = 8\), \(T_a = 6\), \(R =\) Rs 10: bonus Rs 10, wage Rs 70.
Rowan plan (1901)
  • By James Rowan of Glasgow.
  • Guaranteed minimum wage + bonus on part of the time saved.
  • The share paid is the ratio time saved / standard time.
  • Bonus \(= \dfrac{T_s - T_a}{T_s}\,T_a R\). Peaks when \(T_a = T_s/2\).

  • Rowan pays more for small savings, Halsey more once over half the time is saved.
  • Rowan protects against rate-cutting from careless standards.
Emerson efficiency plan
  • By Harrington Emerson. Daily wage guaranteed; standard (100%) from past records.
  • Efficiency \(=\) actual / standard output \(\times 100\).
  • Bonus scale:
    • Below 66.67%: time wage only.
    • 66.67–100%: bonus rising fast to 10% at 90% and 20% at 100%.
    • Above 100%: 20% + 1% per 1% extra.
  • Example: Rs 40/day, standard 50 pins.
    • X 30 pins (60%): Rs 40. Y 50 (100%): Rs 48. Z 60 (120%): Rs 56.
Scanlon plan (group)
  • By Joe Scanlon (USA). Guaranteed time wage.
  • The standard labour-cost-to-sales ratio indexes total labour effectiveness; bonus = the % fall in that ratio.
  • Bonus % \(= \dfrac{L_b/S_b - L_a/S_a}{L_b/S_b} \times 100\) (labour cost / sales).
  • Example: base 1.35 / 12.40 = 10.887%; month 1.45 / 15.50 = 9.355% \(\rightarrow\) bonus 14.07%.
  • With 2.15 lakh labour cost: 13.87% \(>\) base, no bonus.
Priestman plan (group)
  • Bonus % \(= \dfrac{P_a/W_a - P_b/W_b}{P_b/W_b} \times 100\) (output per worker).
  • Example: standard 1200 cars / 500 workers = 2.4. Next month 1400 cars:
    • Same 500 workers \(\rightarrow\) 2.8, bonus 16.67%.
    • 600 workers \(\rightarrow\) 2.333, \(-2.78\%\), no bonus.
Profit sharing
  • Agreed % of annual profit shared with employees (Nepal's Labour Act and Bonus Act require a share of profit as bonus).

column1: Industrial relations; collective bargaining and its process

Industrial relations
  • Relations between management, workers (and their unions) and government in an industry.
  • Aim: industrial peace, higher productivity, fair treatment, no strikes or lockouts.
  • Tools:
    • Collective bargaining; grievance procedure.
    • Joint consultation; workers' participation.
    • Conciliation, arbitration, labour courts.
  • Causes of poor relations:
    • Low wages, bad working conditions.
    • Unfair dismissal.
    • Politically affiliated unions.
    • Poor communication.
  • Nepal: Labour Act 2074, Trade Union Act 2049; frequent politically affiliated strikes.
Collective bargaining
  • Negotiation between employer and a union representing workers on wages, hours, conditions, benefits.
  • Result is a written collective agreement.
Process
  • Deadlock \(\rightarrow\) conciliation, mediation, arbitration.

column1: Chapter 3 — Motivation, Leadership and Entrepreneurship: how is it examined?
column4:
10 hrs  \(\cdot\) asked in all 29 papers  \(\cdot\) 3 units, 21 syllabus topics  \(\cdot\) 591 marks, 25.0% of the archive \(\rightarrow\) about 13 of every 80 marks: usually two full 8-mark questions.
READ THIS FIRST
Asked in every paper, like Ch. 1 and Ch. 2. Three blocks, each with a fixed pattern:
  1. Motivation = “define motivation” (2–3 marks) \(+\) one named theory (5–6 marks). Five theories cover it: Maslow (9 papers), Herzberg (10), Vroom (7), McGregor X-Y (6), ERG as a comparison (6). Learn one figure or table per theory. Content theories (Maslow, ERG, McClelland, Herzberg) say what motivates; process theory (Vroom) says how.
  2. Leadership = qualities of a good leader (12) or styles (11) \(+\) an opinion: “which style suits an engineering project / Nepal / a startup?”. Answer: situational, leaning democratic, with a reason for each context (\(\S\)3.3).
  3. Entrepreneurship = definition + characteristics (8) or “why promote it in Nepal” (7). Always tie the second half to Nepal: jobs, remittance dependence, IT.
Tier chips count papers out of 29: TOP n 8+  HOT n 4–7  PIN n 1–3 inside an 8-mark question  LOW n 1–3, short note only  syllabus, no PYQ yet never set. Bold year = Regular exam.

column1: Define motivation. What are human needs, and how is a need used to motivate? Types of motivation
column4:
• From Latin movere, “to move”; motive = need, want, drive within a person.
  • Definition: the process of stimulating people to act toward goals by creating conditions in which their needs and the organization's goals are satisfied together.
  • Forces within a person that decide the direction, level and persistence of effort at work.
  • Two aspects: knowing human needs; inspiring people to do their best for the enterprise.
Human needs
  • Primary (physiological, safety): food, shelter, security.
  • Secondary (social, esteem, self-actualization): belonging, status, growth.
  • Needs are unlimited, change over time, differ between people, and several operate at once.
Types of motivation
  • Intrinsic: from within; interest, enjoyment, sense of achievement in the task itself. “I want to complete this task.” Lasting.
  • Extrinsic: from outside; pay, bonus, promotion, fear of penalty. “Complete it and be rewarded.”
  • Positive: reward, praise, incentive (carrot).
  • Negative: fear, punishment, threat of dismissal (stick).
  • Financial vs non-financial.
Adhikari's six types, by drive
  • Incentive: rewards, monetary or not, for reaching a target (bonus, promotion): the carrot.
  • Fear: consequences; used when incentives fail: the stick.
  • Achievement: drive for competency; tackle challenges, prove oneself; mostly intrinsic.
  • Growth: burning desire for self-improvement and learning.
  • Power: autonomy over one's own life, or control over others.
  • Social: belong, be accepted, connect with others.
  • No single type works for everyone: personalities differ.
Human needs at work
  • The worker expects:
    • Goals to fulfil.
    • The right to choose a job.
    • Responsibility to reach reasonable goals.
  • The manager must:
    • Understand behaviour.
    • Merge employees' needs with the firm's objectives.
    • Know what satisfies each employee.
    • Build a co-operative climate: an unco-operative, indifferent one kills motivation.
How a need motivates: the need-drive-goal cycle
  • Manager's job: link the employee's unmet need to the organization's goal, so working for the firm satisfies it.
  • A satisfied need no longer motivates; a new one takes its place.
Why motivation is complex
  • Same need \(\rightarrow\) different behaviour in different people.
  • Needs change in kind and intensity.
  • People cannot always express their needs.
  • Many needs act at once.
Importance
  • Higher productivity and quality; better use of resources.
  • Low absenteeism and turnover; fewer grievances.
  • Willing acceptance of change; good relations.
  • Helps employees reach personal goals.
The motivation equation
  • Inputs from the member: time, effort, skills, knowledge.
  • Become performance toward the organization's goals.
  • Which returns outcomes the member values: pay, security, autonomy.
  • Motivation holds only while the outcomes feel worth the inputs.

column1: Techniques of motivation; attitude, group and executive motivation; role of management
column4:
Techniques
  1. Financial: fair wages, bonus, incentives, profit sharing, ESOP.
  2. Meaningful, challenging work: job enrichment, rotation.
  3. Clear targets and measured performance (MBO).
  4. Regular, specific feedback.
  5. Recognition and praise: public appreciation, awards.
  6. Participation in decisions; delegation.
  7. Training, career growth, promotion.
  8. Job security, good working conditions, quality of work life.
  9. Status, healthy competition, flexible hours.
Role of management in motivation
  • Understand each employee's needs; people differ.
  • Create an environment where personal and firm goals meet.
  • Fair pay system; fulfil promised rewards.
  • Give information, training, feedback; act on employee suggestions.
  • Lead by example; make work interesting.
Attitude (self) motivation
  • How a person thinks and feels: self-confidence, belief, positive outlook.
  • Falls with monotonous work, pushy boss, poor health, bad relations, money worries.
  • Cure: interesting job, constructive thinking, build on strengths, adapt.
Group motivation
  • Motivating a team as a unit; team productivity decides success.
  • Needs fairness, honesty, loyalty, tolerance, shared responsibility, constructive criticism.
  • Tools: team goals, group incentives, team building, social recognition.
Executive motivation
  • Keeping managerial talent motivated and in the firm.
  • Executives seek achievement, esteem, self-actualization more than money.
  • Tools: challenging responsibility, autonomy, profit sharing, stock options, status perks, public recognition.
  • Low when: poor boss, blocked advancement, poor pay, insecurity.
Difference (75 Ash)
  • Attitude: the individual's inner state.
  • Group: the team as a whole.
  • Executive: top talent, driven by higher-order needs.
Necessities of group motivation
  • Fairness, truthfulness, honesty, loyalty, stability, tolerance.
  • Ability to take responsibility and co-operate.
  • Constructive criticism; compromise when necessary.
  • Orderliness in mind and action; a sense of humour.
What motivates executives
  • Doing something they can call their own; tasks they set themselves.
  • Seeing what they have done; feeling the job is important.
  • Security; challenge; belief in the value of the work.
  • Higher need for achievement; actualization, esteem, social needs matter more.

column1: Maslow's hierarchy of needs: features, satisfaction-progression, examples
column4:
• Abraham Maslow, 1943. Three propositions:
    • Man is a wanting being: needs are endless.
    • A satisfied need does not motivate; only unmet needs do.
    • Needs form a hierarchy: lower must be largely met before higher ones motivate.
  • Five levels (bottom up), with what the firm gives:
    1. Physiological: food, water, shelter, sleep \(\rightarrow\) adequate wage, rest breaks.
    2. Safety: physical and economic security \(\rightarrow\) safe conditions, job security, insurance, pension.
    3. Social: belonging, friendship \(\rightarrow\) teams, informal groups, events.
    4. Esteem: self-respect, status, recognition \(\rightarrow\) titles, awards, promotion.
    5. Self-actualization: realizing full potential \(\rightarrow\) challenging, creative work, autonomy.
Maslow's pyramid. Lower needs must be met before higher ones motivate.
Satisfaction-progression process (75 Ch)
  • When a need is satisfied, the person progresses to the next higher need, which now motivates.
  • Eg a fresh graduate first wants a salary (physiological), then a permanent post (safety), then a good team (social), then a senior title (esteem), then to start something of their own (self-actualization).
Features and limitations
  • \(+\) Simple, intuitive; widely used by managers.
  • \(-\) Order is not fixed for everyone (an artist may skip safety).
  • \(-\) Several needs act together.
  • \(-\) Hard to measure satisfaction; culture-bound (US study).
  • \(-\) Only one direction (no regression) \(\rightarrow\) ERG fixes this.
Can Maslow explain Laxmi Prasad Devkota's tireless quest? (69 Ch)
  • Only partly. Devkota wrote Muna Madan and his epics while in poverty, debt and grief, and kept writing on his deathbed with cancer.
  • Pure Maslow says unmet physiological and safety needs should have blocked self-actualization.
  • So he contradicts the strict order: self-actualization (creative expression, intrinsic motivation) drove him even with lower needs unmet.
  • Better explained by ERG (needs act together) and intrinsic motivation.
Why some fall from grace while climbing the pyramid (78 Bh)
  • Fraud, crime, suicide among the successful are the irony of the pyramid.
  • Esteem sought by any means: status, wealth, power without ethics \(\rightarrow\) corruption, fraud.
  • Frustration-regression (ERG): blocked at the top, people fall back to greed for material things or to despair.
  • Personal power need (McClelland) outgrows social good.
  • Pressure, isolation, loss of social support \(\rightarrow\) depression, suicide.
  • Maslow's own top level includes morality: those who fall never truly reached self-actualization, they stalled at esteem.
  • Remedy: values and ethics education, social support, fair systems, counselling.

column1: Maslow vs Alderfer's ERG; ERG and Herzberg compared with Maslow; satisfaction-progression vs frustration-regression
column4:
Alderfer's ERG theory (1969)
  • Collapses Maslow's five into three:
    • Existence: physiological + safety.
    • Relatedness: social + external esteem.
    • Growth: internal esteem + self-actualization.
  • Satisfaction-progression: satisfied lower need \(\rightarrow\) move up (as Maslow).
  • Frustration-regression: if a higher need is blocked, the person falls back and wants more of the lower need.
    • Eg an engineer denied promotion (growth) demands higher pay (existence).
  • Several needs can motivate at the same time.
Solid arrows: satisfaction-progression; dashed: frustration-regression; curled: satisfaction-strengthening. The 75 Ch / 69 Ch short note in one picture. Wikimedia Commons (Upul, vectorized by Sushant Savla), CC BY-SA 4.0.
BasisMaslowAlderfer ERG
Levels53
OrderStrict, step by stepFlexible
Needs at onceOne dominantSeveral together
DirectionUp only (progression)Up and down (regression)
BasisClinical observationEmpirical research
Herzberg against Maslow and ERG
  • Herzberg's hygiene factors = Maslow's lower needs = ERG's existence and relatedness.
  • Herzberg's motivators = Maslow's esteem + self-actualization = ERG's growth.
  • Difference: Maslow and ERG say every need motivates when unmet; Herzberg says lower needs only prevent dissatisfaction, never motivate.
  • Maslow and ERG: general human needs. Herzberg: job factors.
ERG at work
  • Existence: basic pay level to buy daily items.
  • Relatedness: good relations, feedback from boss and peers.
  • Growth: a worker who keeps improving skills, creative work.

column1: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y
column4:
• Douglas McGregor, The Human Side of Enterprise (1960): two sets of assumptions managers hold about workers, which shape how they manage.
Theory X (traditional)
  • Average person dislikes work, avoids it.
  • No ambition, avoids responsibility, prefers to be led.
  • Self-centred, indifferent to organizational goals.
  • Resists change; motivated only by money and fear.
  • \(\rightarrow\) Manager must coerce, control, direct, threaten: autocratic style, close supervision.
Theory Y (modern)
  • Work is as natural as play or rest.
  • People exercise self-direction and self-control when committed.
  • Commitment comes from rewards of achievement.
  • They seek responsibility; creativity is widespread.
  • \(\rightarrow\) Manager delegates, involves, enriches jobs: democratic style.
X vs Y against the other theories (72 Ch)
  • X assumes people live at Maslow's lower needs / Herzberg's hygiene level; fits fear-and-punishment theory.
  • Y assumes higher needs and Herzberg's motivators drive people.
  • McGregor favoured Y; modern view: situation decides (contingency).
  • McGregor showed Theory Y managers create more employee engagement.
  • Link to leadership:
    • X \(\leftrightarrow\) autocratic style, close supervision, fear and punishment.
    • Y \(\leftrightarrow\) democratic style, delegation, job enrichment.
  • In the exam, write X and Y as two columns, 6–7 points each.

column1: Herzberg's motivation-hygiene (two-factor) theory: where motivation at work comes from
column4:
• Frederick Herzberg, 1959: interviewed about 200 engineers and accountants in Pittsburgh on times they felt very good or very bad at work.
  • Finding: satisfaction and dissatisfaction come from different factors. The opposite of satisfaction is no satisfaction, not dissatisfaction.
  • Man has two sets of needs: as an animal, to avoid pain; as a human, to grow psychologically.
Hygiene (maintenance) factors: job context
  • Company policy and administration; supervision.
  • Salary; job security; working conditions.
  • Relations with superiors, peers, subordinates; status.
  • Absent \(\rightarrow\) dissatisfaction. Present \(\rightarrow\) only no dissatisfaction, not motivation.
Motivators: job content
  • Achievement; recognition.
  • The work itself (interesting, challenging).
  • Responsibility; advancement; growth.
  • Present \(\rightarrow\) satisfaction and motivation. Absent \(\rightarrow\) no satisfaction (but not dissatisfaction).
So where does motivation at work come from? (80 Bh)
  • From the job itself: achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth. Pay and conditions only remove complaints.
  • Managers: first fix hygiene (else unhappiness), then enrich jobs to motivate.
Criticism
  • Small, professional sample; people credit themselves for good events and blame others for bad (method bias).
  • Pay can be a motivator for low-income workers.
Two separate scales, not one: fixing hygiene moves a worker only to “no dissatisfaction”; only motivators move them toward satisfaction.

column1: Vroom's expectancy (VIE / valency) theory; why it is a process theory; importance of reward
column4:
• Victor Vroom, 1964. A person chooses the behaviour they expect to bring the outcome they value.
  • \[ \text{Motivation } M = E \times I \times V \]
  • Expectancy (E): belief that effort \(\rightarrow\) performance (0 to 1). “If I try, can I do it?”
  • Instrumentality (I): belief that performance \(\rightarrow\) reward. “If I do it, will I be rewarded?”
  • Valence (V): value the person places on that reward. “Do I want it?”
  • Product: if any one is zero, motivation is zero; high only when all three are high.
  • Eg an engineer offered a Dubai posting (V high) for finishing a project early:
    • No effort if the deadline is impossible (E low).
    • No effort if the boss rarely keeps promises (I low).
  • Managers must link rewards to performance and find out which outcomes each worker wants.
Effort \(\rightarrow\) performance \(\rightarrow\) outcomes, and the belief at each link.
Why it is a process theory (80 Bh)
  • It does not list which needs motivate (content theories do).
  • It explains how a person decides: a mental calculation of E, I, V among alternatives.
Importance of reward (74 Ch)
  • Reward sits in two of three terms: it must be valued (V) and reliably linked to performance (I).
  • Managers: offer rewards people want; keep promises; make targets reachable by training and resources (E).

column1: McClelland's theory of learned needs
column4:
• David McClelland (1961): needs are learned from life experience, not inborn; everyone ranks them differently.
  • Achievement (nAch): drive to excel; moderate risks, want feedback, personal responsibility \(\rightarrow\) entrepreneurs.
  • Power (nPow): make others behave as they otherwise would not; personal or social (institutional) power \(\rightarrow\) managers.
  • Affiliation (nAff): friendly, close relations; avoid conflict \(\rightarrow\) team roles.
  • Each need has its own work preferences \(\rightarrow\) managers tailor the environment: high achievers get responsibility, feedback, intermediate risk.

column1: Fear and punishment theory
column4:
• People work to avoid penalties: warnings, fines, demotion, dismissal.
  • Assumes workers are lazy and need pushing (Theory X); the stick of carrot-and-stick.
  • Linked to Skinner's reinforcement: punishment and negative reinforcement.
  • Deterrence:
    • Specific: corrects the offender, stops a repeat.
    • General: punishment made public warns everyone else.
Merits
  • Quick results for discipline, attendance, safety rules.
  • Clear limits: everyone knows the consequence.
Demerits
  • Resentment, fear, low morale.
  • Only minimum effort: people avoid penalty, not seek excellence.
  • Higher turnover; hidden mistakes.
  • Use only as a last resort, fairly and consistently.

column1: Define leadership. Why is it needed? Qualities of a good leader
column4:
• Leadership: the process of influencing people to work willingly toward group or organizational goals, and providing an environment for it.
  • Koontz: “the art or process of influencing people so that they strive willingly and enthusiastically toward the achievement of group goals.”
Why needed
  • Gives vision and direction.
  • Motivates, builds morale and confidence.
  • Coordinates effort; resolves conflict.
  • Leads change; builds culture and teamwork.
  • Represents the group; develops future leaders.
Qualities of a good leader
  1. Vision: knows where to go, sets achievable goals.
  2. Honesty, integrity: same inside and out; trust.
  3. Self-confidence, courage, decisiveness.
  4. Communication: clear speaking, writing, listening.
  5. Human skill: respect, fairness, empathy; credit to others.
  6. Initiative and innovation.
  7. Knowledge, intelligence, judgement.
  8. Discipline, commitment to excellence; leads by example.
  9. Emotional stability, patience, sense of humour.
  10. Calculated risk-taking; learns from mistakes.
  11. Charisma, passion.
  12. Adaptability: changes style with the situation.
What sets a leader apart from regular employees (80 Bh)
  • Vision beyond own job; takes initiative unasked.
  • Owns results, including failures.
  • Influences without formal authority; others follow willingly.
  • Develops others; thinks of the team first.
Adhikari's qualities, with his meaning
  • Guiding vision: knows what to do; pursues it against opposition and failure; sets achievable goals.
  • Passion: believes in the goals; positive outlook others follow.
  • Integrity: knows own weaknesses; promises only what can be kept.
  • Honesty at work and in private life; trust: acts for followers.
  • Curiosity: a learner; risk: calculated, learns from mistakes.
  • Dedication; charisma: maturity, respect, compassion, humour.
  • Listening: “the most important attribute of all”.
Types of leaders, by the source of their lead
  • By position: lead because of the post they hold.
  • By personality: charisma draws followers.
  • By moral example: goodness and integrity inspire.
  • By power held: control over rewards or punishment.
  • Intellectual: lead through knowledge and ideas.
  • By ability to get things done: results earn the lead.

column1: Leadership styles (autocratic, democratic, free-rein); which style suits an engineering project, industry, Nepal, a startup?
column2: 2345678
column4:
• Style = the behaviour pattern a leader adopts toward followers.
Factors affecting style
  • The task: urgent, routine or creative.
  • The tradition of the organization.
  • The type of labour force: skilled or unskilled, followers' maturity.
  • The leader's personality.
  • The time available.
  • Also “gender?”: research finds style differences small and situational.
Power, decision making and communication under the three styles.
  • Autocratic (authoritarian):
    • Leader decides alone, trusts only own competence, gives orders, expects obedience; one-way communication.
    • \(+\) quick decisions, clear control; suits emergencies, unskilled or new staff, military.
    • \(-\) low morale, no creativity, dependence on one person, resentment.
  • Democratic (participative):
    • Leader consults, delegates as far as experience allows, keeps final responsibility; praise and blame shared; two-way.
    • \(+\) better decisions, commitment, morale, creativity; usually most productive.
    • \(-\) slow; needs capable, willing followers.
  • Laissez-faire (free-rein):
    • Leader gives goals and freedom; group decides and self-controls.
    • \(+\) suits experts, researchers; high autonomy.
    • \(-\) no direction, chaos with inexperienced staff.
Other styles
  • Paternalistic: fatherly care for workers' welfare, leader still decides.
  • Bureaucratic: leads strictly by rules and procedures.
  • Transformational: inspires change through vision.
  • Transactional: reward for results, punishment for failure.
Participative management (65 Shr)
  • Employees share in decisions:
    • Suggestion schemes; quality circles.
    • Work committees; worker directors on the board.
  • Importance: commitment, better ideas, fewer disputes, job satisfaction.
Which style for a (modern) engineering project? (78 Bh, 74 Ash)
  • Democratic / participative as the base: engineers are skilled professionals; design choices gain from many views; commitment matters over months.
  • Autocratic moments: safety, deadlines, site emergencies.
  • Free-rein for expert sub-teams (design, R&D).
  • \(\rightarrow\) Situational leadership, democratic by default.
Most effective style in an industrial organization (80 Ba, 68 Ba, 67 Asa)
  • Determine it by: task structure, followers' skill and maturity, leader's power, time pressure (Fiedler, Hersey-Blanchard).
  • Shop floor, routine work, new workers \(\rightarrow\) directive; skilled staff \(\rightarrow\) participative; experts \(\rightarrow\) delegating.
  • Most effective overall: team (9,9) style on Blake-Mouton's grid.
Most efficient in Nepal? (73 Ch)
  • Tradition is autocratic and paternalistic (hierarchy, respect for seniority).
  • Educated young workforce, migration of talent \(\rightarrow\) democratic with a paternalistic touch works best: consult, care for welfare, decide firmly.
  • Government offices need less bureaucracy and more participation.
Nepalese start-ups (82 Ba)
  • Small teams of young, skilled people, fast change, scarce funds.
  • Best: democratic + transformational: shared vision, open ideas, quick consensus, ownership (ESOP), freedom for experts.
  • Founder must switch to decisive (autocratic) mode in a cash or deadline crisis.

column1: Blake and Mouton's managerial grid: styles, examples, significance for growth
column4:
• Robert Blake and Jane Mouton (1964). Two axes, each 1 (low) to 9 (high): concern for production (x) and concern for people (y).
  • Five key styles:
    • (1,1) Impoverished: minimum effort for either; avoids blame. Eg a manager waiting for retirement.
    • (1,9) Country club: comfort and friendliness, weak output. Eg a boss who never enforces deadlines.
    • (9,1) Authority-compliance (task): output through rules and pressure, people ignored. Eg a sweatshop supervisor.
    • (5,5) Middle of the road: balance, adequate results, neither fully met.
    • (9,9) Team: high on both; commitment, trust, shared stake. Eg an agile software team lead.
The leadership grid: concern for production vs concern for people.
Significance for organizational growth (76 Ash)
  • Diagnoses a manager's present style objectively.
  • Shows the target: move toward (9,9).
  • Basis for leadership training (grid seminars).
  • Shows people and production are not a trade-off: both together raise productivity and morale \(\rightarrow\) growth.

column1: Leadership approaches / theories: trait, behavioural, contingency (situational), integrated
column4:
Trait approach
  • Leaders are born, not made (Great Man theory).
  • Identifies traits of effective leaders: drive, leadership motivation, honesty, self-confidence, intelligence, business knowledge, self-monitoring.
  • \(-\) No trait list fits all leaders; ignores followers and situation.
Behavioural approach
  • Leaders are made: what they do matters, and can be learned.
  • Two independent behaviours:
    • Task-oriented: assign work, set standards, push deadlines.
    • People-oriented: trust, respect, welfare.
  • Ohio State and Michigan studies; Blake-Mouton grid.
  • Effective leaders score high on both.
Contingency / situational approach
  • No one best style: it depends on leader, followers and situation.
  • Fiedler: task- or relationship-motivated leader fits situations of different favourableness (leader-member relations, task structure, position power).
  • House's path-goal: leader chooses directive, supportive, participative or achievement-oriented behaviour to clear the path to goals.
  • Hersey-Blanchard: telling, selling, participating, delegating as follower maturity rises.
Integrated approach
  • Combines three sets of variables to choose the effective style:
    • Leader: traits, behaviour, experience.
    • Followers: ability, maturity.
    • Situation: structure, technology, objectives, environment.
  • Most realistic of the four.
Adhikari's three approaches (write if the question says “approach”)
  1. Trait-oriented: leaders born, not made; more intelligent, better educated, stronger power needs, independent, take some risks, self-actualized, hard working, self-confident.
  2. Situational: leadership is a function of the situation, culture, context and customs of the group.
  3. Functional: considers both the individual and the situation; the leader must solve the task problems.
Adhikari's eight leadership theories
  1. Great Man: born to lead; heroic, destined; “man” because leadership was then seen as male, military.
  2. Trait: inherited traits (extraversion, self-confidence, courage).
  3. Contingency: environment variables decide the best style; none best everywhere.
  4. Situational: choose the action by situation (authoritarian when the leader knows most; democratic with skilled experts).
  5. Behavioural: leaders are made; learnable by teaching and observation.
  6. Participative: takes others' input; leader keeps the right to decide.
  7. Management (transactional): supervision, organization, group performance; rewards and punishments.
  8. Relationship (transformational): inspires by showing the higher good of the task; wants each member to fulfil potential; high ethics.

column1: Leader vs manager; boss vs leader; “a reader is a leader”; challenges for a modern leader; you as a future leader
column4:
BasisManagerLeader
Power fromPosition (authority)Personal influence
FocusThings, systems, controlPeople, vision, inspiration
MottoDo things rightDo the right things
WorkPlan, organize, budgetSet direction, align, motivate
ChangeMaintains orderDrives change
FollowersSubordinatesFollowers
  • A good manager should be a leader; a leader need not be a manager.
Boss vs leader (73 Ch)
  • Boss = autocratic style:
    • Commands, uses fear; says “I”; says “Go!”.
    • Takes credit, blames others for failure.
  • Leader = democratic / transformational style:
    • Guides, inspires; says “we”; says “Let's go!”.
    • Shares credit, owns failure.
“A reader is a leader” (71 Ch)
  • Reading builds:
    • Knowledge (expert power).
    • Vision and judgement from others' experience.
    • Communication: vocabulary, clear expression.
  • Informed leaders can switch styles wisely: consult as a democrat, decide as an autocrat when needed.
  • Eg Gandhi, Mandela, Gates: lifelong readers.
Challenges for a modern leader (75 Ch)
  • Rapid technological change; remote and diverse teams.
  • Talent retention (migration in Nepal); ethics, transparency.
  • Uncertainty (pandemic, politics); information overload.
Me as a future leader (75 Ash, 75 Ch)
  • Start as a technically strong engineer; build human skills.
  • Lead by example, listen, share credit, keep learning.
  • Aim for a (9,9) team style, adapting to the situation.
Managers vs leaders, function by function
  • Both do the same four activities: planning, organizing, directing, controlling. They do them differently (right).
  • Manager: focus on things, do things right, follows the rules.
  • Leader: focus on people, do the right things, inspires, shapes entities.

column1: Authority and power
column4:
• Authority: legitimate right to command, from the position.
    • Flows downward; accepted as rightful.
    • Lost when the post is left.
  • Power: ability to influence behaviour, from any source.
    • Can exist without authority (an informal leader).
    • Can flow in any direction.
Sources of power (French and Raven)
  • Legitimate: from the position.
  • Reward: can give pay, promotion, praise.
  • Coercive: can punish.
  • Expert: knowledge and skill.
  • Referent: personal charisma; people want to identify with the leader.

column1: Entrepreneurship: meaning, development, characteristics of an entrepreneur
column4:
• From French entreprendre, “to undertake”.
  • Entrepreneurship: the capacity and willingness to spot an opportunity, organize resources and run a new venture, bearing its risk, for profit and value.
  • Schumpeter: entrepreneurs are innovators: new products, new methods, new markets, new sources of supply, new organization.
  • Schumpeter: “Entrepreneurs are business leaders and not simple owners of capital. They are men of vision, drive and talent, who spot out opportunities and promptly grasp them for exploitation.”
  • McClelland: a nation's growth depends on its people's need for achievement more than on natural resources.
  • The word first meant an organizer of musical or other entertainments; from the early 18th century it meant business.
Functions of an entrepreneur
  1. See an opportunity.
  2. Organize the enterprise.
  3. Raise capital.
  4. Hire labour.
  5. Arrange materials.
  6. Select managers.
  7. Bear the risk and uncertainty.
Entrepreneurship development
  • Entrepreneurs are made: Entrepreneurship Development Programmes (EDPs), in steps:
Factors influencing it
  • Components of creativity: need for achievement, independence, power; family background.
  • Originality; flexibility; fluency of ideas.
  • Sensitivity to problems and the ability to redefine them.
Characteristics of an entrepreneur
  1. Initiative and self-starting.
  2. Opportunity seeking; foresight.
  3. Calculated (moderate) risk-taking: not a gambler.
  4. Creativity and innovation.
  5. High need for achievement; competitive.
  6. Self-confidence, optimism.
  7. Commitment, persistence: learns from failure.
  8. Decision making; administrative ability.
  9. People skills, communication, leadership.
  10. Technical and business knowledge.
  11. Hard work, discipline, strong work ethic.
  12. Flexibility; handles uncertainty.
Adhikari's list of 12 (short-note version, 79 Bh)
  • Administrative capability; creativity.
  • Self-confidence; optimism.
  • Human relations; communication.
  • Foresight; clarity of objectives.
  • Technical knowledge; secrecy.
  • Decision making; willingness to take risk.

Role in economic development / why promote
  • Employment and self-employment.
  • Capital formation: mobilizes idle savings.
  • Innovation, new products, technology.
  • Balanced regional development; decentralization.
  • Equitable income distribution.
  • Exports, import substitution \(\rightarrow\) foreign exchange.
  • Better use of local resources; higher GDP and tax revenue.
  • Raises living standards; inspires others.
Why Nepal and its government must promote it
  • Over a million youths leave for foreign jobs; remittance-dependent economy.
  • Huge trade deficit; low industrial base.
  • Unused resources: hydropower, tourism, agriculture, herbs, IT.
  • Tools: startup loans, incubation, tax holidays, one-window registration, skills training, access to credit.
Creativity alone is not enough: a conducive environment (79 Ba, 73 Shr)
  • Political stability and consistent policy.
  • Access to finance: banks, venture capital, collateral-free loans.
  • Infrastructure: power, roads, internet.
  • Easy registration, low red tape, fair tax.
  • Market access, skilled labour, education, incubators.
  • Culture that accepts failure and risk.
Significance of law enforcement (73 Ch)
  • Protects property and intellectual property.
  • Enforces contracts \(\rightarrow\) trust in business deals.
  • Fair competition; controls cartels and corruption.
  • Investor confidence \(\rightarrow\) capital flows in.

column1: Entrepreneurship in Nepal's IT sector; would you start a startup; risks and challenges; Silicon Valley

Role in Nepal's IT sector (76 Ash)
  • IT services exports (outsourcing, software) earn foreign currency with little capital.
  • Jobs for graduates at home, slowing brain drain.
  • Digital services: payments (eSewa, Khalti), ride sharing (Pathao), e-commerce (Daraz), ed-tech.
  • Solutions for local problems in agriculture, health, government.
Would I start one after graduation? (74 Ch)
  • Yes, with preparation: gain 2–3 years' industry experience and savings, validate the idea, find a co-founder, start lean.
  • Or no: if family needs steady income or the idea is untested. Either answer works if justified.
Risks and challenges for an aspiring entrepreneur in Nepal
  • Small domestic market; low purchasing power.
  • Scarce seed and venture capital; banks want collateral.
  • Restrictions on international payments and foreign investment in small amounts.
  • Policy instability, bureaucracy, strikes.
  • Talent loss to migration; social stigma of failure.
  • Weak IP protection; infrastructure gaps outside cities.
Silicon Valley: the best example (69 Ch)
  • Stanford University research + venture capital + risk-taking culture + skilled migrants + network effects.
  • Produced Apple, Google, Intel, HP; failure accepted as learning.
  • Lesson for Nepal: link universities, investors and startups in clusters.

column1: What is a case study? Why are case studies conducted? Objectives and value of case study
column4:
Meaning
  • A case = written description of a real management situation: facts, reports, even opinions, but no evaluation.
  • Case study method: learners analyse the case, identify problems, weigh alternatives and decide, as a manager would.
  • Belief behind it: managerial competence comes from studying and discussing actual situations, not only theory.
  • Word means different things to different users:
    • lawyer: a legal case;
    • researcher: a vehicle for testing a hypothesis;
    • management education: an authentic problem to train analysis and decision making.
  • Aim secured by facing the learner with a whole series of cases, not one.
  • Harvard Business School made it the standard method of management teaching (1920s) verified/added.
Why conducted (AJ Sir)
  • Teach managerial skills: analyse a situation, frame the right questions, find answers, make decisions.
  • Link the three foundations of management practice: research, theory, practice.
Objectives
  1. Impart knowledge and facts about real organizations.
  2. Develop problem analysis skill: separate symptoms from causes.
  3. Develop decision-making skill under incomplete information.
  4. Improve communication: discuss, defend, write reports.
  5. Shape attitude: nothing in human behaviour is absolutely right or wrong; respect other views.
  6. Apply theory to practice; test principles against reality.
  7. Build teamwork and judgement through group discussion.
Value (short note, 66 Bh)
  • \(+\) realistic, active learning.
  • \(+\) develops analytical thinking; learner participates.
  • \(+\) many solutions welcome \(\rightarrow\) no single “right” answer.
  • \(+\) bridges classroom and industry.
  • \(-\) time consuming: gathering, arranging and writing up the facts is long and tedious.
  • \(-\) needs a skilled discussion leader.
  • \(-\) one case may not generalize.
Case study vs lecture verified/added
LectureCase study
Learnerlistensanalyses, decides
Contentprinciplesreal situation
Answerone correctseveral defensible
Skill builtrecalljudgement, communication

column1: Types of case studies
column4:
By research purpose
  • Illustrative: descriptive; one or two instances show what a situation is like; makes the unfamiliar familiar; gives readers a common language.
  • Exploratory (pilot): short study before a large investigation, to find the right questions and measures. Risk: early findings released as conclusions.
  • Cumulative: combines past studies from several sites and times \(\rightarrow\) wider generalization at no new cost.
  • Critical instance: one or a few sites of unique interest, or to challenge a universal claim; answers cause-effect questions.
Teaching cases
  • Incident: a short event to react to.
  • Problem / decision: choose an action.
  • Appraisal: evaluate a situation.
  • Descriptive: shows how a firm handled something.

column1: Explain the phases and steps of case study, with an example from your field
column4:
Five phases (group discussion)
Notes on the phases
  • Phase 1: every member reads the case alone first; a group that has not read cannot discuss.
  • Phase 2: facts are organized by relevance to the decision; irrelevant detail is dropped.
  • Phase 3: some cases supply the critical questions; otherwise the group phrases them. A wrongly defined problem wastes the rest.
  • Phase 4: each sub-group presents its strongest argument; decisions are then debated openly.
  • Phase 5: the lesson is transferred beyond this one case.
  • The discussion leader (teacher) guides but does not give the answer.
Six steps (individual analysis)
Notes on the steps
  • Step 1: read the case and its questions, then write in one line what the case is about and what action or answer is required.
  • Step 2: arrange facts systematically; mark which are facts and which are opinions of people in the case.
  • Step 3: treat first ideas as tentative; give every alternative due consideration before rejecting it.
  • Step 4: choose one solution, the best answer on the given data.
  • Step 6 checklist: what does it achieve? what difficulties? what limits (time, money, equipment, manpower)? is it the best alternative?
  • A solution that fails the checklist sends you back to step 3.
Phases vs steps: which to write
  • Phases = how a group works through a case in a class or workshop (discussion method).
  • Steps = how one analyst solves it and writes it up (report method).
  • Question says “phases” \(\rightarrow\) 5 phases; “steps” \(\rightarrow\) 6 steps; “phases and steps” (81 Bh) \(\rightarrow\) both lists, 2 marks each.
  • Always add one line of example from engineering (below).
Analysing a case problem (AJ Sir): the reading order before step 1
  1. Read the title of the case.
  2. Note the company and the case problems as given.
  3. Careful, detailed reading of the whole case.
  4. Meet the central characters: who decides, who is affected.
  5. Define the problems, then develop the solution.
Example from engineering: why did a hydropower project finish two years late? verified/added
StepApplied
1 State the problem60 MW project, planned 4 years, took 6; cost overrun 40%. Why, and how to prevent it next time?
2 Collect and analyse dataSchedule vs actual (Gantt), change orders, land-acquisition dates, contractor payments, site logs, interviews with engineers and locals. Finding: land dispute (8 months), tunnel geology surprise (10 months), late payments \(\rightarrow\) contractor slowdown.
3 Tentative solutions(a) better geological survey; (b) settle land before tender; (c) escrow payment to contractor; (d) matrix project organization with one accountable manager.
4 Recommended solutionCombine (a)+(b) as pre-construction gates, (c) for cash flow; (d) as the structure.
5 Written reportBackground, problem, data, analysis, recommendations, implementation plan.
6 ChecklistAchieves on-time completion; needs upfront survey budget; limit: political land issues; still the best alternative.

column1: Prepare a case study of an organization (NEA / Nepal Telecom; your college) following the case structure
column4:
Case report writing methodology
  1. Organizational background:
    • goals and objectives; formation;
    • structure; social needs and value;
    • historical relation; financial position.
  2. Identification of the problem.
  3. Hypothesis: the suspected cause.
  4. Case research design: what data, from whom, how.
  5. Collection and analysis of data.
  6. Generalization and interpretation.
  7. Conclusions and recommendations.
Typical report titles (a full O&M case study)
  1. Acknowledgement.
  2. Organization: history, objectives, input, process, output.
  3. Organization structure (chart).
  4. Form of ownership.
  5. Personnel policies; manpower planning.
  6. Recruitment and selection; training and development.
  7. Job evaluation; merit rating; wages and incentives.
  8. Motivation; marketing; leadership; MIS.
  9. Drawbacks; suggestions and recommendations.
  10. Conclusion; references.
  • The titles are the syllabus itself: a case study is where Ch. 1–3 and 5 are applied to one real organization.
Writing the 8-mark version in the exam
  • Use the 7 headings of the methodology as your headings; 1–3 lines each.
  • Spend the marks on what the question names: 72 Ch names planning horizon, leadership, motivation, HRD \(\rightarrow\) one analysis paragraph each.
  • Give one or two real numbers (loss %, load-shedding hours, pass rate); they show the data step was done.
  • Draw one figure: an org chart, a cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram, or a time-bound plan.
  • End with recommendations + time frame, then the checklist line (achieves, difficulties, limits, best alternative).
  • Roughly: background 1, problem + hypothesis 1, design + data 2, analysis 2, recommendations 2 marks.

column1: Define MIS. Why is MIS needed? Its functions and importance
column4:
• The three words:
    • Management: directing an enterprise toward objectives (planning, organizing, coordinating, controlling).
    • Information: processed, orderly selected data that gives knowledge for decisions.
    • System: interacting procedures forming an organized whole.
  • MIS: “a system of obtaining, abstracting, storing and analysing data to produce information for planning, controlling and decision making, given to managers at the time they can best use it.”
  • Henry C. Lucas: “a set of organized procedures which, when executed, provide information to support decision making.”
  • Uses computing and communication technology; draws on internal and external sources; covers past, present and projected activity.
Functions
  1. Data capture: from internal and external sources.
  2. Processing: classify, calculate, compare, summarize.
  3. Storage and retrieval.
  4. Determining information needs: what, how much, when, for whom.
  5. Evaluation and abstraction: judge reliability, edit, condense.
  6. Dissemination: right information, right manager, right time.
  7. Prediction, planning, control support.
Adhikari's four, with his questions
  • Determination of needs: what? how much? how, when, by whom?
  • Evaluation: how much confidence can be placed in it?
  • Abstraction: editing and reducing incoming information.
  • Dissemination: right information, right manager, right time.
The information system inside the organization, inside its environment
The organization's information system within its environment.
Need for MIS
  • Every manager decides on information; more complex firms \(\rightarrow\) more data than a person can handle.
  • Production managers: production, labour, machine, overhead costs; capacity.
  • Marketing managers: sales trends, market research, selling costs, new products.
  • Personnel managers: turnover, absenteeism, skills, wage levels, labour market.
  • Why MIS in addition to task software (79 Ba): payroll, billing, inventory packages each serve one task; MIS integrates their data into summary and exception reports across the firm, for decisions no single package supports.
Importance
  • The “heart” of the firm: timely, relevant information for decisions.
  • Measures performance against goals \(\rightarrow\) control.
  • Supports planning, forecasting, coordination across departments.
  • Reduces uncertainty and cost of information; keeps it current.
  • Stores confidential information securely for future use.
  • Competitive advantage: faster response to market.
  • Eg a bank's MIS flags branches whose loan defaults exceed target; an airline's reservation data sets fares by demand.
  • Also:
    • Brings new facts to management's notice.
    • Supplies information at a reasonable cost.
    • Focuses on decisions with an attractive benefit/cost ratio.
    • Supplies reliable, logical data for every management function.

column1: Data vs information vs knowledge vs wisdom; how data and information are used in an office
column4:
• Data: raw, unprocessed facts and figures; no meaning alone. Eg 45, 62, 38.
  • Information: data processed into a meaningful, useful form. Eg “average daily sales this week: Rs 48,000, down 12%”.
  • Knowledge: information combined with experience and understanding: knows how. Eg “sales drop every exam month”.
  • Wisdom: applying knowledge with judgement to decide well: knows why and what is best. Eg “run a student discount in exam months”.
  • DIKW pyramid (right): each level adds context and value. verified/added
The contrast in detail
  • Data:
    • Uninterpreted raw statement of facts.
    • Non-random symbols (words, values, figures) representing what has happened.
    • From research or observation. Eg payroll, bank statement.
  • Information:
    • Facts organized to give the desired knowledge.
    • Data interpreted and understood by the recipient.
    • Can mean different things to different people.
Qualities of good information
  • Accurate; timely; complete; concise.
  • Relevant; at the right frequency; understandable.
  • Worth its cost: costs less than its value.
DIKW pyramid. Wikimedia Commons (Longlivetheux), CC BY-SA 4.0.
Data becomes information through processing, with feedback.
Use in an office (78 Bh, 75 Ash)
  • Data recorded daily: attendance, invoices, receipts, stock movements, letters.
  • Processed into information: payroll, monthly accounts, stock reports, pending-file lists.
  • Used for: paying staff, ordering supplies, answering customers, monitoring work, reporting to management, planning budgets.

column1: Role of information in the planning process and in decision making; information system is vital for planning and control
column4:
Information system for planning
  • Planning answers: where are we? where do we want to go? how do we get there? when? who? how much will it cost?
  • MIS supplies:
    • Past performance: where we are.
    • Forecasts of demand, costs, market, technology: where to go.
    • Resource data: how, who, at what cost.
  • Long-range (3–5 year) plan \(\rightarrow\) yearly operating plan \(\rightarrow\) individual targets: MIS tracks each.
  • Planning is continuous; MIS keeps the plan a “living document” by feeding actual results back.
Information system for decision making
  • Decision = choosing the best alternative; more and better information \(\rightarrow\) better choice.
  • Steps supported:
    1. Identify the problem: exception reports.
    2. Generate alternatives: data, models.
    3. Evaluate: what-if analysis, DSS.
    4. Choose the best.
    5. Monitor: feedback reports.
  • Strategic: future-oriented, long range, unstructured: new plant, new market.
  • Tactical: short term: budgets, fund flow, personnel problems, product improvement.
  • Operational: structured, routine: inventory, scheduling, allocating workers.
Vital for control (68 Ch)
  • Control = compare actual with plan \(\rightarrow\) correct. Without timely information there is nothing to compare.
  • Exception reports highlight only deviations (management by exception).
Value of MIS in the planning process (76 Ch, 76 Ash)
  • Accurate forecasts of demand, cost, prices.
  • Realistic targets based on past performance.
  • Scenario analysis: what if sales fall 10%?
  • Early warning when plans slip.
  • Coordination of departmental plans from one shared database.

column1: Hierarchy of information needs; organizational structure and MIS; MIS at different levels of management
column4:
• Managers at different levels need different kinds of information at different intervals: the hierarchy of information needs. MIS is a pyramid matching the organization's levels.
  • Operational (lower): day-to-day production of goods and services.
    • Detailed, internal, precise, historical data.
    • Hourly or daily: raw material needs, work schedules, output vs schedule.
  • Tactical (middle): puts top's plans into operation.
    • Summaries: schedules, revenue, profit, cost, other economic measures.
    • Weekly or monthly; used to set controls and allocate resources.
  • Strategic (top): corporate policy, growth, survival.
    • Aggregated, future-oriented, much of it external (competitors, suppliers, consultants, media).
    • Quarterly or yearly: are goals met, is the firm profitable, what should change.
  • Bottom of the pyramid: transaction processing data feeding all levels.
  • For “MIS at different levels” (80 Ba), draw the pyramid in \(\S\)5.3: system type by level, across the functional areas.
Level of management and information content: policies, plans, budgets at the top; revenue, profit, costs, measurements, schedules in the middle; goods, services, performance at the bottom. S.K. Joshi, Fig. 3.3.
Why the hierarchy is necessary (68 Ch)
  • Each level gets only what it needs: no overload at top, no gaps below.
  • Detail is condensed upward (reports), direction flows downward (plans).
  • Matches decision type to information type.
Organizational structure and MIS
  • Nature of the firm (profit or not, goods or services, single site or global) decides its information needs and systems.
  • MIS draws on organization concepts: structure, communication, power, decision making, motivation, leadership.
  • Adhikari: MIS is a pyramid of four levels of information resources: strategic, tactical, operational control, transaction processing. Since decisions are specific to levels, so are information needs.

column1: Information architecture
column4:
• From Greek archos (chief) + tekton (carpenter): design and structure.
  • Information architecture = how the parts of an information system interconnect and communicate: the general flow of information, how databases interrelate, and how applications make access easier for managers.
  • Also (AJ Sir): organizing, structuring and labelling content so users find information and complete tasks.
  • Anthony's triangle: strategic, tactical, operational applications stacked by level.
  • Add divisions (production, marketing, accounting) \(\rightarrow\) a two-dimensional structure (figure below).
    • Each division keeps its unique data.
    • Common events (a sale) create shared data \(\rightarrow\) a shared corporate database.
  • Traditional bureaucracy: information flows up, over, down; divisions rarely talk directly. Good architecture removes these barriers.
Anthony's triangle extended across divisions: side A and side B data meet in shared data. S.K. Joshi, Fig. 3.6.

column1: Classification of information systems (TPS, MIS, DSS, ESS) and their support to managers; DSS vs MIS; EIS for top managers
column4:
• Information system: hardware, software, data, people and procedures that produce information for day-to-day, short-range and long-range activities.
TPS
  • Captures and processes data from day-to-day transactions: deposit, payment, order, reservation. Serves the operational level.
  • Two modes:
    • Online: each transaction processed at once (deposits, reservations); most TPS today.
    • Batch: transactions grouped and run later (paychecks, invoices); efficient for bulk.
MIS: three kinds of report
  • Accurate, timely, organized information to decide, solve problems, supervise, track progress; reports regularly, so also management reporting system.
  • Detailed: confirms each transaction. Eg detailed order report.
  • Summary: totals, tables, graphs. Eg inventory summary.
  • Exception: only what is out of range. Eg items below reorder level.
A payroll TPS: master file, payroll system, cheques, reports, general ledger.
TPS files (orders, materials, ledger) feed MIS files and reports to managers.

Level servedOperationalMiddle (management)Middle, professionalsTop (strategic)
InputsTransactions, eventsSummarized transaction dataTransaction data + models, external dataAggregate internal + external data

DSS vs MIS (78 Bh, 75 Ash)
BasisMISDSS
PurposeRoutine reporting, controlSupport a specific decision
ProblemsStructuredSemi-/unstructured

How production managers use DSS in addition to MIS (82 Bh)
  • MIS tells what happened: output, scrap, machine downtime reports.
  • DSS asks what if: best production schedule and product mix (linear programming), make-or-buy, capacity expansion, inventory reorder levels, maintenance timing, with simulations of cost and delay.
Significance of EIS for top managers (79 Ba)
  • One-screen dashboards of key indicators; drill-down to detail.
  • External data: competitors, markets, economy.
  • Fast, easy to use without technical skill.
  • Supports strategic decisions and early warning; less dependence on staff reports.
TPS feeds MIS and DSS; all feed ESS.
Support to managers
  • TPS: records every transaction; the data source for all others.
  • MIS: regular detail, summary and exception reports \(\rightarrow\) control (also called management reporting system).
  • DSS: models + data to decide non-routine problems.
  • ESS: strategic view for top managers.
  • Expert system: knowledge base + inference rules imitate an expert (Eg medical or fault diagnosis).
  • Modern software integrates them (ERP): firms consolidate TPS, MIS and DSS into one integrated system.
DSS: data from inside and outside
  • Internal: sales, manufacturing, inventory, finance.
  • External: interest rates, population trends, construction costs, raw material prices.
  • Eg a voyage-estimating DSS runs models over ship, port, fuel and charter-cost files.
Expert system: how it reasons
  1. User describes the situation.
  2. Inference rules make logical judgements.
  3. Knowledge base holds experts' knowledge and experience.
  4. System gives advice or a decision.

column1: Information support for functional areas of management; how MIS is used at different levels
column4:
Four functional areas (columns) crossed with three levels (rows): each cell is the information system that supports it.
Sales and marketing
  • TPS: order processing, invoicing.
  • MIS: sales by region, salesperson, product; sales management.
  • DSS: pricing, sales region analysis, promotion planning.
  • ESS: 5-year sales trend forecast, market share.
Manufacturing and production
  • TPS: material movement, machine control, purchase orders.
  • MIS: inventory control, production scheduling reports, quality and scrap.
  • DSS: production planning, relocation cost, capacity.
  • ESS: 5-year operating plan, new plant decisions.
Finance and accounting
  • TPS: payroll, accounts payable and receivable, general ledger.
  • MIS: annual budgeting, cost reports.
  • DSS: profitability, contract cost analysis, investment appraisal.
  • ESS: profit planning, long-term financing.
Human resources
  • TPS: employee record keeping, attendance.
  • MIS: turnover, absenteeism, training reports, appraisal history.
  • DSS: compensation analysis, manpower allocation.
  • ESS: personnel (manpower) planning.

column1: Computers and MIS; role of computers in MIS; what is a website
column4:
• Computers are the means of modern MIS, not MIS itself: a computer alone does not make work efficient; identify the management problem first.
  • Before computers information was: too late, incomplete, costlier than its worth, unfocused, irrelevant, rigid.
  • Role of computers:
    • Fast, accurate processing of huge data.
    • Storage and quick retrieval.
    • Reports in any format, on demand.
    • Communication across sites.
    • Models and simulation for decisions.
  • Quick-response systems:
    • Online processing: manager interacts directly with the computer.
    • Real-time processing: system runs alongside the activity and guides it (Eg ATM, airline booking).
    • Time sharing: many users share one computer at high speed.
  • Two uses: data (transaction) processing with fixed reports, and end-user computing (managers, staff using spreadsheets, queries) with flexibility.
  • Relationship: MIS defines what information is needed; the computer produces it quickly and cheaply. Computer = tool, MIS = purpose.
  • Website (74 Ash): a set of linked web pages under one domain name, hosted on a server and reached through the internet. verified/added
    • Publishes information to customers.
    • Collects orders and feedback (data).
    • Gives staff remote access to reports.
  • Computer-aided advertising (69 Ch, short note LOW 1 69 Ch): verified/added
    • Computer graphics and design for ads.
    • Targeted online, email and social media ads.
    • Analytics of clicks and conversions.

column1: Database information system
column4:
• Database: organized collection of related data serving many applications at once, appearing to be in one place.
  • Kinds:
    • Personal database: an individual's contacts, schedules, notes.
    • Corporate database: large, shared, integrity critical.
  • DBMS: software to create, maintain and query it (Oracle, MySQL); applications extract data without their own files.
  • Components:
    • Data dictionary: describes the data.
    • Architecture: relations between data.
    • The objects described; rules for manipulation.
  • Advantages: no redundancy, consistency, sharing, security, easy reporting.
  • Examples:
    • A bank's customer database used by accounts, loans, ATM and mobile banking.
    • A college's student database used by admission, exams, library, fees.

column1: Networking information system
column4:
• Telecommunication network linking computers and terminals so users at different locations share data and resources.
  • Components: computers, terminals, channels, communication processors, software; common rules = protocols; analog or digital signals.
  • Types:
    • By area: LAN (a building), MAN (a city), WAN (country or world).
    • By users: internet (public), intranet (staff only), extranet (staff plus partners, suppliers).
  • Needs a flexible, standard network architecture that grows with the business.
  • Advantages: real-time sharing, distributed offices, e-commerce, email, lower cost.
  • Eg bank branches and ATMs on one network; NEA billing linked across offices.

column1: How information systems can be organized properly
column4:
• Complete centralization: one central IS department holds hardware, software, data and MIS personnel; serves all user departments.
    • \(+\) control, standards, economy of scale, security.
    • \(-\) slow response, users feel distant, bottleneck.
  • Complete decentralization: each department has its own systems and MIS staff.
    • \(+\) responsive, users own their systems.
    • \(-\) duplication, incompatible data, higher cost.
  • Hybrid (distributed): central database and standards, local processing and staff. Most common today.
    • \(+\) control of shared data with local responsiveness.
    • \(-\) needs clear rules on who owns what.
Other means of organizing it properly
  • Steering committee of senior managers sets IS priorities.
  • CIO (chief information officer) at top level.
  • Clear policies for data ownership, access and security.
  • Standards for hardware, software, data formats.
  • User training and a help desk.
  • Regular audit and review of the system.
Roles of an organized MIS department
  • Hardware administration; database administration.
  • Software development and support.
  • End-user support and training.
  • Computing standards; corporate data access.
  • Advocacy: promotes IS use across the firm.

column1: Evolution of MIS
column4:
1. Manual ledgers and punch cards.
  2. Electronic data processing (1950s–60s): record keeping.
  3. MIS reports (1960s–70s).
  4. DSS (1970s): models, operations research.
  5. EIS / ESS (1980s).
  6. PCs and end-user computing: graphical, user-friendly interfaces.
  7. Networks, ERP: integrated systems.
  8. Internet, cloud and business intelligence.
  • Driven by: growth of management theory, management science, new production methods and structures, and computers.
